title: IP-KVM Hardware on a Corporate Laptop and on Its Network Segment
summary: USB and PnP telemetry for the KVM-over-IP and video-capture hardware DPRK operators attach to employer-issued laptops, paired with the network view of the same devices: Raspberry Pi hardware addresses, the default TinyPilot host name and internet-exposed KVM interfaces.
description: A KVM-over-IP device gives an overseas operator console control of a laptop below the operating system, with nothing for an EDR agent to inspect. Huntress recovered a PiKVM V4 Mini and a Guermok USB capture card, registered as a webcam, on a laptop within hours of its reaching a residential address; ReliaQuest documents the equivalent TinyPilot artifacts.

The hardware still enrols: Windows writes a key under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB and raises Security event 6416, while macOS lists it in system_profiler and leaves a ColorSync display profile behind. A capture card proves nothing alone; its co-occurrence with an IP-KVM on one host is the pattern both vendors call out.

The network view covers what the agent never sees: Raspberry Pi address prefixes in DHCP and ARP (mattysplo.it), the default tinypilot.local name (ReliaQuest), and exposed interfaces from Shodan or Censys matched against proxy logs (Grumpy Goose Labs). A GL.iNet Comet with an obfuscation preset presents another identity, so a clean result does not rule one out.
logic: Collect: USB/PnP enrolment on Windows (6416, PnP connect) and macOS (USB inventory, ColorSync profiles); process, DNS and ARP/DHCP data
Match: USB descriptor, serial or VID/PID of a known IP-KVM or capture card (PiKVM, TinyPilot, GL.iNet Comet, NanoKVM, Guermok)
Match: or a ColorSync profile, command line or DNS name carrying tinypilot, pikvm or glkvm
Match: or (optional) a Raspberry Pi or TinyPilot MAC prefix in DHCP leases or the ARP cache
Report: hosts with a match, newest first; flag hosts that match both an IP-KVM and a capture card
technique_scope: Hardware-based remote access to a corporate endpoint, evading software remote-access controls entirely (MITRE ATT&CK T1200, Hardware Additions), in support of fraudulent-employment valid-account misuse (T1078); network-side discovery of the same hardware.

indicators.note: PiKVM Composite Device, as recovered by Huntress; the same VID/PID is published for TinyPilot by mattysplo.it. It is the generic Linux USB gadget identifier, so it also appears on any other Linux device emulating USB peripherals.
Under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB (Huntress).
Guermok USB3 Video capture card, registered as a webcam on the host (Huntress).
Under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB (Huntress).

The same Guermok capture card enumerates on some hosts under the names of the chipset vendors behind it, UltraSemi and MacroSilicon (the MS2130 that VID_345F&PID_2130 identifies), rather than under Guermok, so every query on this page matches those strings alongside it. Recorded from this site's own observation on 18 September 2026 rather than from published reporting.
NanoKVM, which enumerates as USB 3346:1009 (SANS Internet Storm Center, "Detecting IP KVMs").
PiKVM mass-storage interface as seen in USB logging (ReliaQuest).
TinyPilot DeviceDescription as seen in USB logging (ReliaQuest).
Manufacturer string a stock TinyPilot reports (Grumpy Goose Labs).
Manufacturer string a stock PiKVM reports (Grumpy Goose Labs).

The GL.iNet Comet's manufacturer string, which changed between firmware versions (Grumpy Goose Labs, "Be KVM, Do Fraud"). The Comet ships presets that impersonate other peripherals, so a device that presents these strings has not had them turned on; see the Comet hunt for the fingerprints that survive the presets.
Comet USB configuration descriptor name (Grumpy Goose Labs, "Be KVM, Do Fraud").
Default PiKVM gadget serial (ReliaQuest, mattysplo.it).
Default TinyPilot gadget serial (ReliaQuest, mattysplo.it). The hex decodes to "keymimepi", after Key Mime Pi, the project TinyPilot builds on.

Colour profile macOS writes for the display TinyPilot presents (ReliaQuest). It persists after the device is unplugged, which makes it the one artifact in this hunt that finds a KVM which is no longer attached.
"A new external device was recognized by the System." Huntress recommends alerting on this event where the device description contains PiKVM or Guermok.
Hardware-address prefixes published by mattysplo.it. The first is attributed to TinyPilot itself; the remainder are Raspberry Pi, which is what a PiKVM and a TinyPilot are both built on.
Default TinyPilot mDNS name (ReliaQuest). Link-local, so a hit means the device is on the same segment as the host that resolved it.
TinyPilot administration over SSH from the connected host (ReliaQuest).
TinyPilot service control (ReliaQuest).
Shodan/Censys query for an internet-exposed PiKVM web interface (mattysplo.it).
Shodan/Censys query for an exposed Guacamole remote-desktop gateway (mattysplo.it).
Combined Shodan query for both device web interfaces (Grumpy Goose Labs).

queries.query:
// Hunt: IP-KVM and capture-card hardware on a corporate laptop. Windows PnP,
// macOS colour profiles, and any command line or lookup naming tinypilot.
let KvmWords = dynamic(["pikvm", "tinypilot", "glkvm", "cafebabe", "6b65796d696d657069"]);
let CaptureWords = dynamic(["guermok", "ultrasemi", "macrosilicon"]);
union
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and ActionType == "PnpDeviceConnected"
  | extend Raw = tostring(AdditionalFields)
  | extend Class = case(
      Raw has_any (KvmWords)
        // optional: generic Linux USB gadget id, shared by any board emulating peripherals
        or Raw contains "VID_1D6B&PID_0104"
        // optional: GL.iNet also sells routers and travel hubs
        or Raw has "glinet"
        or Raw contains "VID_3346&PID_1009", "IP-KVM",
      // optional: capture cards are common alone; they only matter next to an IP-KVM
      Raw has_any (CaptureWords) or Raw contains "VID_345F&PID_2130", "CaptureCard",
      "")
  | where Class != ""
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Class, Signal = "usb-enrolment", Evidence = Raw ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
  | where FolderPath contains "/ColorSync/Profiles/Displays"
  | where FileName has_any ("tinypilot", "pikvm", "glkvm")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Class = "IP-KVM", Signal = "colorsync-profile", Evidence = FileName ),
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and RemoteUrl has "tinypilot"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Class = "IP-KVM", Signal = "tinypilot-lookup", Evidence = RemoteUrl ),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and ProcessCommandLine has "tinypilot"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Class = "IP-KVM", Signal = "tinypilot-command", Evidence = ProcessCommandLine )
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Classes = make_set(Class),
            Signals = make_set(Signal), Evidence = make_set(Evidence, 10) by DeviceName
| extend KvmAndCapture = set_has_element(Classes, "IP-KVM") and set_has_element(Classes, "CaptureCard")
| sort by KvmAndCapture desc, LastSeen desc
queries.note: A host listing both Classes (IP-KVM and CaptureCard) is the pairing Huntress reports; confirm the AdditionalFields keys against a known PnpDeviceConnected event in your tenant.

queries.query:
FROM logs-system.security-*, winlogbeat-*, logs-endpoint.events.file-*, logs-endpoint.events.process-*, logs-endpoint.events.network-*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 90 days
| EVAL usb = TO_LOWER(CONCAT(COALESCE(winlog.event_data.DeviceDescription, ""), " ", COALESCE(winlog.event_data.DeviceId, "")))
| EVAL other = TO_LOWER(CONCAT(COALESCE(file.path, ""), " ", COALESCE(process.command_line, ""), " ", COALESCE(dns.question.name, "")))
| EVAL class = CASE(
    event.code == "6416" AND usb RLIKE ".*(pikvm|tinypilot|glkvm|cafebabe|6b65796d696d657069|vid_3346&pid_1009).*", "IP-KVM",
    event.code == "6416" AND usb RLIKE ".*(guermok|ultrasemi|macrosilicon|vid_345f&pid_2130).*", "CaptureCard",
    other RLIKE ".*(/colorsync/profiles/displays/.*(tinypilot|pikvm|glkvm)|tinypilot).*", "IP-KVM",
    "")
| EVAL class = CASE(class != "", class, event.code == "6416" AND usb RLIKE ".*vid_1d6b&pid_0104.*", "IP-KVM", "")
| EVAL class = CASE(class != "", class, event.code == "6416" AND usb RLIKE ".*glinet.*", "IP-KVM", "")
| WHERE class != ""
| STATS first_seen = MIN(@timestamp), last_seen = MAX(@timestamp), classes = COUNT_DISTINCT(class) BY host.name
| SORT classes DESC, last_seen DESC
queries.note: Reads the Windows 6416 event plus Elastic Defend file, process and network events; classes = 2 marks the IP-KVM and capture-card pairing.

queries.query:
// Hunt: IP-KVM hardware. xdr_data carries the colour-profile, command-line and DNS matches; USB enrolment is not in it.
dataset = xdr_data
| filter (event_type = ENUM.FILE and action_file_path ~= "(?i)/ColorSync/Profiles/Displays/" and action_file_name ~= "(?i)tinypilot|pikvm|glkvm")
    or (event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)tinypilot")
    or (event_type = ENUM.NETWORK and (dns_query_name ~= "(?i)tinypilot" or action_external_hostname ~= "(?i)tinypilot"))
| alter signal = if(event_type = ENUM.FILE, "colorsync-profile", if(event_type = ENUM.PROCESS, "tinypilot-command", "tinypilot-lookup"))
| comp min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen, values(signal) as signals by agent_hostname
| sort desc last_seen
queries.note: Covers the three matches xdr_data records on both operating systems; USB enrolment needs the Windows event or osquery queries.

queries.query:
-- Hunt: IP-KVM hardware on macOS (Linux for the USB and ARP branches); osquery has no usb_devices table on Windows.
SELECT 'usb-device' AS signal, vendor || ' ' || model || ' ' || serial || ' ' || vendor_id || ':' || model_id AS evidence
FROM usb_devices
WHERE vendor || model LIKE '%PiKVM%'
   OR vendor || model LIKE '%TinyPilot%'
   OR vendor || model LIKE '%GLKVM%'
   OR (vendor_id = '3346' AND model_id = '1009')
   OR serial IN ('CAFEBABE', '6b65796d696d657069')
   OR (vendor_id = '1d6b' AND model_id = '0104')  -- optional: generic Linux gadget id, shared by any board emulating peripherals
   OR vendor LIKE '%Glinet%'  -- optional: GL.iNet also sells routers and travel hubs
   OR (vendor_id = '345f' AND model_id = '2130') OR vendor || model LIKE '%Guermok%' OR vendor || model LIKE '%UltraSemi%' OR vendor || model LIKE '%MacroSilicon%'  -- optional: capture cards are common alone
UNION ALL
SELECT 'colorsync-profile', path || ' (created ' || btime || ')'
FROM file
WHERE (path LIKE '/Library/ColorSync/Profiles/Displays/%' OR path LIKE '/Users/%/Library/ColorSync/Profiles/Displays/%')
  AND (filename LIKE '%TinyPilot%' OR filename LIKE '%PiKVM%' OR filename LIKE '%GLKVM%')
UNION ALL
-- optional: Raspberry Pi and TinyPilot MAC prefixes in the ARP cache; every Pi on the segment matches
-- (macOS prints octets without the leading zero, so 04:c9:8b and e4:5f:01 each appear twice)
SELECT 'arp-neighbour', address || ' ' || mac
FROM arp_cache
WHERE mac LIKE '04:c9:8b:%' OR mac LIKE '4:c9:8b:%' OR mac LIKE 'b8:27:eb:%' OR mac LIKE '28:cd:c1:%'
   OR mac LIKE 'd8:3a:dd:%' OR mac LIKE 'dc:a6:32:%' OR mac LIKE 'e4:5f:01:%' OR mac LIKE 'e4:5f:1:%'
   OR mac LIKE '2c:cf:67:%' OR mac LIKE '3a:35:41:%' OR mac LIKE '88:a2:9e:%' OR mac LIKE '98:fe:54:%';
queries.note: Local state check for macOS and Linux endpoints: attached USB devices, ColorSync profiles that persist after a KVM is unplugged, and neighbours with Raspberry Pi prefixes.

false_positive_notes: VID_1D6B&PID_0104 is the generic Linux gadget identifier, shared by any Linux board emulating USB peripherals. Treat it as a lead and rely on the FriendlyName and serial, which are stock values that can be changed.

Out-of-band hardware is legitimate in labs and datacenters, so scope this to standard-issue laptops; a capture card alone is unremarkable for anyone who streams. An IP-KVM on a remote employee's laptop is the strong signal.

Raspberry Pi prefixes cover every Pi, including hobbyist Pi-hole and smart-home devices on home networks, so the network checks yield leads rather than alerts. Refresh the prefix list, as new blocks are issued.

Shodan and Censys queries find exposed KVMs generally, most unrelated to this campaign; Grumpy Goose Labs notes one on your network means the system is probably reachable unintentionally, not misused.

title: IP-KVM Hardware Hiding Behind Spoofed USB Descriptors
summary: Catches an IP-KVM whose vendor, product and serial strings have been renamed to something innocuous, using the USB configuration descriptor and interface shape the device cannot change without ceasing to work.
description: The descriptors in the preceding hunt are strings the device chooses to report, and a PiKVM's are editable. Grumpy Goose Labs found that the USB configuration descriptor survives a stock rename, reading "Config 1: PiKVM device" on a PiKVM and "Config 1: ECM device" on a TinyPilot, and joins the connection event through the descriptor-set hash.

The same research reads the interface count and the maximum power draw beside it, and chelmzy.tech hunts on a base class presented with audio and mass-storage interfaces rather than on any name. Both devices also default to a Linux monitor identifier on the HDMI connection, which is itself an artefact.

TinyPilot's knowledge base tells Windows users to rename its sound device to Toshiba-H2C in mmsys.cpl. That per-endpoint registry override leaves both the suggested string and the untouched USB device instance path underneath it for a sweep to find.
logic: Collect: USB configuration descriptors and device enrolment (Windows, macOS), plus Windows audio-endpoint registry writes
Match: configuration name is 'Config N: PiKVM device' or 'Config N: ECM device', or the default serial CAFEBABE or 6b65796d696d657069
Match: or an audio endpoint value under MMDevices\Audio set to Toshiba-H2C, TinyPilot or PiKVM, or carrying the TinyPilot serial
Match: or (optional) gadget id VID_1D6B&PID_0104, 5 or more interfaces, or 3 or more PnP setup classes on one device
Report: hosts and devices with a match, newest first
technique_scope: Hardware addition (MITRE ATT&CK T1200) with masquerading of the device identity (T1036) to defeat name-based USB allowlisting and detection.
data_sources: EDR USB descriptor and device-class telemetry

indicators.note: ConfigurationDescriptorName reported by a PiKVM, surviving a rename of the vendor and product strings (Grumpy Goose Labs).
ConfigurationDescriptorName reported by a TinyPilot (Grumpy Goose Labs).
The published match, written loosely because the configuration number has been observed changing (Grumpy Goose Labs).

Hash over vendor id, product id and serial that joins the descriptor event to the connection event. Shared across devices with identical configuration, so it identifies a configuration rather than a physical device (Grumpy Goose Labs).
Interface count. A device whose claimed identity does not account for five interfaces is worth pulling (Grumpy Goose Labs).
Base class presented together with audio and mass-storage interfaces on one composite device (chelmzy.tech).
Base class with a mass-storage interface, particularly where the reported device name has no mass-storage function (chelmzy.tech).

The name TinyPilot's own documentation instructs Windows users to give the TinyPilot audio endpoint in mmsys.cpl so that it stops appearing under the product name. The string is arbitrary and an operator is free to pick another; what makes this one worth matching is that the instruction is public, concrete and widely read, so the same value recurs across unrelated machines.

Where the rename lands. Under each Render and Capture endpoint, the Properties key holds the endpoint name in {a45c254e-df1c-4efd-8020-67d146a850e0},2, which mmsys.cpl edits, alongside the adapter description in {b3f8fa53-0004-438e-9003-51a46e139bfc},6 and the device instance path in {b3f8fa53-0004-438e-9003-51a46e139bfc},2, which it does not.

Fixed serial every TinyPilot presents, written by /opt/tinypilot-privileged/init-usb-gadget and documented by the vendor; the hex decodes to "keymimepi". It appears in the device instance path of the audio endpoint the rename is meant to disguise, which is why the sweep below reads that path rather than the displayed name.

queries.query:
// Hunt: IP-KVM with renamed USB strings. Default serials survive a rename; so does the audio-endpoint
// rename TinyPilot documents (Toshiba-H2C).
union
// optional: one hardware id enrolling under 3 or more setup classes, which approximates a composite KVM; webcams, headsets and docks match too
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and ActionType == "PnpDeviceConnected"
  | extend Fields = parse_json(AdditionalFields)
  | extend HardwareId = extract(@"(VID_[0-9A-Fa-f]{4}&PID_[0-9A-Fa-f]{4})", 1, tostring(Fields.DeviceId))
  | where isnotempty(HardwareId)
  | summarize Timestamp = max(Timestamp), Classes = make_set(tostring(Fields.ClassName)) by DeviceName, HardwareId
  | where array_length(Classes) >= 3
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "three-setup-classes", Evidence = strcat(HardwareId, " ", tostring(Classes)) ),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and ActionType == "PnpDeviceConnected"
  | extend Raw = tostring(AdditionalFields)
  | where Raw has_any ("cafebabe", "6b65796d696d657069")
      // optional: generic Linux USB gadget id, shared by any board emulating peripherals
      or Raw contains "VID_1D6B&PID_0104"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "default-serial-or-gadget-id", Evidence = Raw ),
( DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
  | where RegistryKey contains @"CurrentVersion\MMDevices\Audio"
  | where RegistryValueData contains "Toshiba-H2C" or RegistryValueData has_any ("tinypilot", "pikvm", "6b65796d696d657069")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "audio-endpoint-rename", Evidence = strcat(RegistryValueName, " = ", RegistryValueData) )
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Signals = make_set(Signal), Evidence = make_set(Evidence, 10) by DeviceName

title: GL.iNet Comet IP-KVM Behind Its Built-In Obfuscation Profiles
summary: Fingerprints for the GL.iNet Comet, an IP-KVM whose firmware ships with ready-made presets that impersonate a Logitech, Corsair, Dell or Microsoft peripheral, and for the configuration descriptor, display identity and hardware address those presets leave untouched.
description: Earlier hunts treat a spoofed identity as something an operator does to a PiKVM or TinyPilot after purchase; GL.iNet's Comet inverts that. Grumpy Goose Labs records built-in obfuscation profiles that in one step rewrite the USB vendor and product strings and identifiers and swap the HDMI EDID, presenting a Logitech receiver, a Corsair, Dell or Microsoft keyboard.

The presets leave the USB configuration descriptor name, "Glinet device" on firmware 1.5.0 and "Config 1: GLKVM device" on 1.3.0, which anchors this hunt. The serial CAFEBABE, 125 milliamps and seven interfaces under every profile corroborate it, since a wireless keyboard presenting seven interfaces is not what its name says.

On the network, GL.iNet's own documentation gives glkvm.local, the KVMCloud service at glkvm.com, and Tailscale, ZeroTier or NetBird access under the machine name glkvm. Grumpy Goose Labs also records the hardware address prefix 94:83:C4 and reads it from the ARP caches an EDR already collects.
logic: Collect: USB descriptors and enrolment (Windows, macOS), DNS and connection records, DHCP leases and ARP neighbours
Match: configuration name 'Glinet device' or 'Config 1: GLKVM device', or stock strings GLKVM, Glinet, GLIKVM, Composite KVM Device
Match: or serial CAFEBABE with the gadget id or a spoofed Logitech, Corsair, Dell or Microsoft VID/PID
Match: or a DNS name or connection containing glkvm (glkvm.local, glkvm.com, glkvm.<tailnet>.ts.net)
Match: or (optional) 7 interfaces at 125 mA, or MAC prefix 94:83:C4, 80:34:28 or 48:DA:35 in DHCP or ARP
Report: hosts with a match, newest first
technique_scope: Hardware addition (MITRE ATT&CK T1200) with vendor-supplied masquerading of the device identity (T1036), in support of fraudulent-employment valid-account misuse (T1078).
data_sources: EDR USB descriptor and device-class telemetry

indicators.note: ConfigurationDescriptorName on Comet firmware 1.5.0. Grumpy Goose Labs records it unchanged under all four of the firmware's built-in obfuscation profiles, which is what makes it the anchor for this hunt rather than the vendor and product strings those profiles rewrite.

ConfigurationDescriptorName on Comet firmware 1.3.0 (Grumpy Goose Labs). Match both forms: the naming changed between the two firmware releases the research covers, and a fleet will hold devices on either.
DeviceManufacturer in the stock configuration only (Grumpy Goose Labs). Every obfuscation profile replaces this string, so a miss here says nothing.
DeviceProduct in the stock configuration on both firmware versions (Grumpy Goose Labs). Also the DeviceProduct a stock PiKVM reports, per the first hunt in this series.

DeviceSerialNumber recorded for the Comet in the stock configuration and under all four obfuscation profiles (Grumpy Goose Labs). The same value is the default PiKVM gadget serial, so it identifies the class of device rather than the vendor.

Stock Comet device instance identifier on both firmware versions (Grumpy Goose Labs). This is the generic Linux USB gadget identifier, shared with PiKVM and TinyPilot and with any other Linux board emulating USB peripherals, so it is a lead rather than an attribution.

Logitech Unifying Receiver, presented by the Comet under built-in obfuscation profile 1 alongside DeviceManufacturer "Logitech Inc" (Grumpy Goose Labs). A real Unifying Receiver is commonplace; what is not is one whose configuration descriptor reads "Glinet device".
Presented under obfuscation profile 2 alongside DeviceManufacturer "Corsair" and DeviceProduct "Corsair Gaming RGB" (Grumpy Goose Labs).
Dell Computer Corp. Multimedia Pro Keyboard, presented under obfuscation profile 3 (Grumpy Goose Labs).

Microsoft Corporation Wireless Multimedia Keyboard, presented under obfuscation profile 4 (Grumpy Goose Labs). This profile spoofs the USB identity alone; the research records no substitute display identity with it.

Interface count recorded for the Comet on firmware 1.5.0; 4 on 1.3.0 (Grumpy Goose Labs). A keyboard or a wireless receiver has no reason to present seven interfaces, which is what makes this the numeric corroboration for a spoofed identity.

WmiMonitorID instance name for the EDID a stock Comet presents over HDMI: ManufacturerName GLI, UserFriendlyName GLIKVM, SerialNumberID 891247, week 8 of 2021, running 2560 x 1440 at 59 Hz (Grumpy Goose Labs).

indicators.value: GLKVM (#- HD Audio Driver for Display Audio)
indicators.note: Display-audio endpoint a stock Comet mounts (Grumpy Goose Labs). Under an obfuscation profile the endpoint is named after the substituted display instead, so read the list rather than matching this string alone.

Hardware address prefix observed for the Comet and included in the ARP-neighbour query Grumpy Goose Labs publishes. The research is explicit that prefixes in that list may also cover travel routers from the same manufacturers, and GL.iNet's main business is travel routers.
Prefixes carried by the ARP-neighbour query Grumpy Goose Labs publishes for the other KVM devices its research surveys (JetKVM and NanoKVM); they are not Comet prefixes.

Default mDNS name, from GL.iNet's own documentation rather than from the research: "Enter glkvm.local in the address bar." Link-local, so a host that resolves it is on the same segment as the device. This is the GL.iNet counterpart to tinypilot.local in the network-presence hunt.

Vendor cloud service GL.iNet calls KVMCloud, documented by GL.iNet as the site a bound device is reached through after signing in with a GL.iNet account. It is the manufacturer's legitimate service, not attacker infrastructure; its value to a defender is that a corporate endpoint or a corporate network has no ordinary reason to reach it.

GL.iNet documents Tailscale, ZeroTier and NetBird as alternative remote-access paths enabled from an Apps Center on the device, and gives glkvm.tail1fd0.ts.net as the example Tailscale name. The tailnet portion is per-account; the stable part is the machine name glkvm. An operator taking this path never touches glkvm.com at all.

queries.query:
// Hunt: GL.iNet Comet, stock or running an obfuscation profile (the serial and VID/PID pair survive the profiles).
let SpoofIds = dynamic(["VID_1D6B&PID_0104", "VID_046D&PID_C526", "VID_6940&PID_6973", "VID_413C&PID_2011", "VID_045E&PID_005F"]);
union
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and ActionType == "PnpDeviceConnected"
  | extend Raw = tostring(AdditionalFields)
  | where Raw has_any ("GLKVM", "Glinet", "GLIKVM", "GLIC21C") or Raw contains "Composite KVM Device"
      or (Raw has "CAFEBABE" and Raw has_any (SpoofIds))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "usb-or-display-enrolment", Evidence = Raw ),
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and RemoteUrl has "glkvm"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "glkvm-lookup", Evidence = RemoteUrl )
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Signals = make_set(Signal), Evidence = make_set(Evidence, 10) by DeviceName
| sort by LastSeen desc
queries.note: Defender does not surface the USB configuration descriptor, so this finds the stock strings and the serial-plus-VID/PID pair; the descriptor name needs Falcon.

queries.query:
title: GL.iNet Comet IP-KVM Recognized by a Corporate Endpoint
id: 35f97668-42dc-5aa5-a0ff-3f0d60a06792
status: experimental
description: >
  Detects Windows recognizing a GL.iNet Comet IP-KVM, by the stock vendor and
  product strings or by the default serial CAFEBABE paired with the generic
  gadget id or one of the four peripheral identities the firmware's built-in
  obfuscation profiles present. Hardware of this class hands an operator
  console control of the host below the operating system, so the enrolment
  event is often the only endpoint-side signal.
references:
  - https://blog.grumpygoose.io/be-kvm-do-fraud-8ab523d26c9d
  - https://docs.gl-inet.com/kvm/en/faq/local_access_via_browser/
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection_event:
    EventID: 6416
  selection_description:
    DeviceDescription|contains:
      - 'GLKVM'
      - 'Glinet'
      - 'GLIKVM'
      - 'Composite KVM Device'
  selection_serial:
    DeviceId|contains: 'CAFEBABE'
  selection_ids:
    DeviceId|contains:
      - 'VID_1D6B&PID_0104'
      - 'VID_046D&PID_C526'
      - 'VID_6940&PID_6973'
      - 'VID_413C&PID_2011'
      - 'VID_045E&PID_005F'
  condition: selection_event and (selection_description or (selection_serial and selection_ids))
falsepositives:
  - Out-of-band management hardware legitimately deployed in a lab, test bench or datacenter
  - Composite KVM Device is also the product string a stock PiKVM reports, so it identifies the class of device
level: high
queries.note: Matches the Windows Security 6416 enrolment event for the stock strings or for the serial with a gadget or spoofed identity.

queries.query:
```Placeholders: index=wineventlog is WinEventLog:Security (event 6416); index=edr is your EDR USB, process, DNS and connection events; index=dhcp is DHCP leases.```
((index=wineventlog EventCode=6416) OR index=edr)
    ("GLKVM" OR "Glinet" OR "GLIKVM" OR "GLIC21C" OR "Composite KVM Device"
     OR ("CAFEBABE" AND ("VID_1D6B&PID_0104" OR "VID_046D&PID_C526" OR "VID_6940&PID_6973" OR "VID_413C&PID_2011" OR "VID_045E&PID_005F")))
| stats min(_time) AS first_seen max(_time) AS last_seen values(sourcetype) AS sources BY host
```optional: GL.iNet, JetKVM and NanoKVM MAC prefixes in DHCP; GL.iNet's main business is travel routers, so 94:83:C4 matches those too. Delete from here to the closing bracket to drop it.```
| append
    [ search index=dhcp
      | eval mac_clean=lower(replace(mac, "[:.-]", ""))
      | eval oui=substr(mac_clean, 1, 6)
      | search oui IN ("9483c4", "803428", "48da35") OR hostname="*glkvm*"
      | stats min(_time) AS first_seen max(_time) AS last_seen values(ip) AS addresses
              values(hostname) AS hostnames BY mac_clean ]
| sort - last_seen
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
queries.note: Free-text matching over raw events, so it works without field extractions on the Windows event and EDR data.

tuning.reason: the GL.iNet prefix covers its travel routers, and JetKVM and NanoKVM prefixes are not Comet prefixes

queries.note: The configuration name survives every built-in obfuscation profile, so a config-name hit is the anchor result.

FROM logs-system.security-*, winlogbeat-*, logs-endpoint.events.network-*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 90 days
| EVAL usb = TO_LOWER(CONCAT(COALESCE(winlog.event_data.DeviceDescription, ""), " ", COALESCE(winlog.event_data.DeviceId, "")))
| EVAL signal = CASE(
    event.code == "6416" AND usb RLIKE ".*(glkvm|glinet|glikvm|composite kvm device).*", "stock-strings",
    event.code == "6416" AND usb RLIKE ".*cafebabe.*" AND usb RLIKE ".*(vid_1d6b&pid_0104|vid_046d&pid_c526|vid_6940&pid_6973|vid_413c&pid_2011|vid_045e&pid_005f).*", "serial-and-spoofed-id",
    TO_LOWER(COALESCE(dns.question.name, "")) RLIKE ".*glkvm.*", "glkvm-lookup",
    "")
| WHERE signal != ""
| STATS first_seen = MIN(@timestamp), last_seen = MAX(@timestamp), signals = VALUES(signal) BY host.name
| SORT last_seen DESC
queries.note: Reads the Windows 6416 event and Elastic Defend DNS events; signals names the artifact that fired.

queries.query:
// Hunt: GL.iNet Comet. xdr_data carries the glkvm lookup; USB descriptors are not in it.
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.NETWORK and (dns_query_name ~= "(?i)glkvm" or action_external_hostname ~= "(?i)glkvm")
| comp min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen, values(dns_query_name) as lookups by agent_hostname

queries.query:
-- Hunt: GL.iNet Comet on macOS and Linux (usb_devices does not exist on Windows).
SELECT 'usb-device' AS signal, vendor || ' ' || model || ' ' || serial || ' ' || vendor_id || ':' || model_id AS evidence
FROM usb_devices
WHERE vendor LIKE '%GLKVM%' OR vendor LIKE '%GLIKVM%' OR vendor LIKE '%Glinet%' OR model LIKE '%Composite KVM Device%'
   OR (serial = 'CAFEBABE' AND ((vendor_id = '1d6b' AND model_id = '0104') OR (vendor_id = '046d' AND model_id = 'c526')
       OR (vendor_id = '6940' AND model_id = '6973') OR (vendor_id = '413c' AND model_id = '2011')
       OR (vendor_id = '045e' AND model_id = '005f')))
UNION ALL
-- optional: GL.iNet, JetKVM and NanoKVM MAC prefixes in the ARP cache; travel routers match 94:83:c4
SELECT 'arp-neighbour', address || ' ' || mac
FROM arp_cache
WHERE mac LIKE '94:83:c4:%' OR mac LIKE '80:34:28:%' OR mac LIKE '48:da:35:%'
queries.note: Local check on macOS and Linux for the stock strings, the serial with a spoofed identity, and ARP neighbours with KVM-vendor prefixes.

tuning.reason: 94:83:c4 covers GL.iNet travel routers and the other prefixes are other vendors' KVMs
tuning.remove: delete from the -- optional comment through the end of the statement and the UNION ALL above it

false_positive_notes: Grumpy Goose Labs can neither confirm nor deny DPRK use of these devices, and the Comet is a mainstream product. Scope to standard-issue laptops and treat a hit as a question.

Several indicators are weak alone: the VID/PID, CAFEBABE and Composite KVM Device are shared with PiKVM, and the spoofed identities are real peripherals. 94:83:C4 covers GL.iNet's whole line, mostly travel routers.

Firmware values date from releases 1.3.0 and 1.5.0 of November 2025, so a later release may change the descriptor name and the hunt needs re-baselining. GL.iNet documents no default password, unlike TinyPilot.

title: Unmanaged Remote-Access and RMM Tooling on Employee Endpoints
summary: A fleet-wide sweep for the consumer remote-access and RMM software DPRK IT workers install to hand control of an employer-issued laptop to an operator overseas, with a per-device product count that flags the hosts running four or more of them.
description: Where an operation has not gone as far as hardware, it reaches the laptop through ordinary remote-access software. Mandiant records GoToRemote/LogMeIn, GoToMeeting, Chrome Remote Desktop, AnyDesk, TeamViewer and RustDesk on victim laptops; Unit 42 adds Splashtop; ReliaQuest ranks AnyDesk, RustDesk, VS Code tunnelling and Chrome Remote Desktop; Microsoft adds JumpConnect and AnyViewer.

The signal is not that these tools exist, since many are legitimate IT software, but that one appears where it was never sanctioned, usually within days of issue. One tool is ambiguous; DTEX rates four or more on one endpoint as warranting investigation, and Mandiant advises monitoring for multiple remote-administration tools.

Zscaler adds an AnyDesk tampering signal: operators edit pwd_hash, pwd_salt and token_salt in its configuration to set an unattended-access password without the interactive dialog. The queries cover Windows and macOS in one list; the Cortex XQL query adapts Unit 42's published sweep.
logic: Collect: process starts and file writes on Windows and macOS endpoints
Match: image is a remote-access client (AnyDesk, TeamViewer, RustDesk, Splashtop, ScreenConnect, GoTo, AnyViewer, Jump Desktop, others)
Match: or a Chrome Remote Desktop extension id in a profile path, or AnyDesk config (service.conf, user.conf) written by another process
Exclude: devices of IT-support and managed-service staff (replace the placeholder list)
Report: devices with their distinct products, most first; escalate 4 or more (DTEX)
technique_scope: Remote Access Tools abuse (MITRE ATT&CK T1219, T1219.002) on a corporate endpoint held by a fraudulently hired employee (T1078).
data_sources: macOS application bundles and launchd configuration

indicators.value: AnyDesk, RustDesk, TeamViewer, AnyViewer, Chrome Remote Desktop, Splashtop, GoToRemote/LogMeIn, GoToMeeting, JumpConnect, ScreenConnect, VS Code dev tunnels
indicators.note: Named across Mandiant, Unit 42, ReliaQuest and Microsoft reporting on DPRK IT-worker operations; ScreenConnect is one of the products in the Unit 42 sweep.
Chrome Remote Desktop extension, as matched in Unit 42's published sweep.
Chrome Remote Desktop extension, as matched in Unit 42's published sweep.
Code-signing vendor Unit 42's query maps to RustDesk.

indicators.value: FleetDeck Inc, SimpleHelp Ltd, NetSupport Ltd, Atera Networks, ConnectWise LLC/Inc, Splashtop Inc
indicators.note: Signing vendors Unit 42's query uses in place of process names.
AnyDesk configuration values operators set directly to enable unattended access without the interactive password dialog (Zscaler).

queries.query:
// Hunt: unmanaged remote-access and RMM tooling. Names are matched without .exe, so the Windows and macOS binaries share one list.
let ExcludedDevices = dynamic([]);  // replace with the device names of IT-support and managed-service staff
let Tools = datatable(Name:string, Product:string) [
  "anydesk", "AnyDesk",
  "teamviewer", "TeamViewer",
  "teamviewer_service", "TeamViewer",
  "tv_w32", "TeamViewer",
  "tv_x64", "TeamViewer",
  "rustdesk", "RustDesk",
  "remoting_host", "Chrome Remote Desktop",
  "srservice", "Splashtop",
  "srmanager", "Splashtop",
  "splashtopstreamer", "Splashtop",
  "splashtop streamer", "Splashtop",
  "meshagent", "MeshCentral",
  "ateraagent", "Atera",
  "client32", "NetSupport",
  "pcilic", "NetSupport",
  "pcideply", "NetSupport",
  "screenconnect.clientservice", "ScreenConnect",
  "connectwisecontrol.client", "ScreenConnect",
  "screenconnect client", "ScreenConnect",
  "g2comm", "GoToMeeting",
  "gotoassist", "GoToRemote/LogMeIn",
  "lmiguardiansvc", "GoToRemote/LogMeIn",
  "lmi_rescue", "GoToRemote/LogMeIn",
  "aeroadmin", "AeroAdmin",
  "dwrcs", "DameWare",
  "supremo", "Supremo",
  "winvnc", "UltraVNC",
  "tvnserver", "TightVNC",
// optional: Quick Assist ships with Windows and is routine in support sessions
  "quickassist", "Quick Assist",
  "fleetdeck_agent", "FleetDeck",
  "simplehelpcustomer", "SimpleHelp",
  "zohoassist", "Zoho Assist",
  "action1_agent", "Action1",
  "nomachine", "NoMachine",
  "anyviewer", "AnyViewer",
  "jumpconnect", "JumpConnect",
  "jump desktop connect", "JumpConnect"
];
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
  | extend Name = replace_string(tolower(FileName), ".exe", "")
  | lookup Tools on Name
  | where isnotempty(Product)

title: Visual Studio Code Dev Tunnels Used as Remote Access
summary: A developer laptop can be handed to a remote operator with no third-party software at all, using the tunnelling feature built into Visual Studio Code. ReliaQuest ranks it among the tools North Korean operators use most.
description: VS Code's tunnelling feature publishes a machine to a Microsoft-hosted relay, reachable from a browser or another VS Code instance and authenticated by a GitHub or Microsoft account the employer does not control. It needs no installer, inbound firewall rule or unfamiliar binary, and the parent process is the editor the employee is meant to use.

ReliaQuest lists VS Code tunnelling among the most popular remote-access methods of North Korean IT workers, sometimes alongside an IP-KVM, and Unit 42's sweep covers it. This hunt looks for the tunnel subcommand on Windows and macOS, the code_tunnel.json file and macOS launch agent a tunnel leaves, and traffic to the Microsoft relay.
logic: Collect: process starts, file creations and relay lookups or connections on Windows and macOS endpoints
Match: command line runs the tunnel subcommand (code or code-tunnel with 'tunnel', 'code tunnel', or vscode.dev/tunnel)
Match: or code_tunnel.json is created under .vscode-cli, or the macOS launch agent com.visualstudio.code.tunnel.plist is written
Match: or (optional) the relay (*.devtunnels.ms, rel.tunnels.api.visualstudio.com) is contacted on 3 or more days
Report: devices with a match, newest first
technique_scope: Remote Access Tools abuse through a legitimate developer tool (MITRE ATT&CK T1219) with command-and-control over a trusted third-party relay (T1102, T1572).

indicators.note: Subcommand that publishes the host to the relay (Unit 42, ReliaQuest).
Created in the user's home profile when a VS Code tunnel is established, on Windows and macOS alike (MITRE ATT&CK, IDE Tunneling detection strategy).
Launch agent that code tunnel service install registers so the tunnel survives logout and reboot, in the system or a user LaunchAgents directory.
Browser entry point to a published tunnel (Unit 42).
Microsoft dev tunnel service endpoints. Microsoft's VS Code documentation names only the relay control endpoint below, so verify this wildcard against your own proxy logs before relying on it.

Dev tunnel relay control endpoint, named in Microsoft's VS Code documentation as the domain to allow or deny to control the feature. The queries match the rel.tunnels.api.visualstudio.com suffix so that a prefix other than global still matches.

queries.query:
// Hunt: VS Code dev tunnel as remote access (Windows and macOS).
union
// optional: relay contact on 3 or more days; a developer debugging remotely does the same
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl contains "devtunnels.ms" or RemoteUrl contains "rel.tunnels.api.visualstudio.com"
  | summarize Timestamp = max(Timestamp), ActiveDays = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1d)) by DeviceName
  | where ActiveDays >= 3
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "relay-3-days", Evidence = tostring(ActiveDays) ),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where (FileName in~ ("code.exe", "code-tunnel.exe", "code", "code-tunnel") and ProcessCommandLine has "tunnel")
      or ProcessCommandLine contains "code tunnel"
      or ProcessCommandLine contains "vscode.dev/tunnel"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "tunnel-command", Evidence = ProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d) and ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
  | where (FileName =~ "code_tunnel.json" and FolderPath contains ".vscode-cli")
      or (FileName =~ "com.visualstudio.code.tunnel.plist" and FolderPath contains "/Library/LaunchAgents")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "tunnel-artifact-file", Evidence = strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName) )
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Signals = make_set(Signal), Evidence = make_set(Evidence, 10) by DeviceName
| sort by LastSeen desc
queries.note: Rows are devices with a tunnel command or artifact; relay-3-days alone is a lead until a command or artifact backs it.

| EVAL signal = CASE(signal != "", signal, relay RLIKE ".*(devtunnels[.]ms|rel[.]tunnels[.]api[.]visualstudio[.]com)", "relay-lookup", "")
| WHERE signal != ""
| STATS first_seen = MIN(@timestamp), last_seen = MAX(@timestamp), signals = VALUES(signal) BY host.name
| SORT last_seen DESC
queries.note: Reads Elastic Defend process, file and DNS events; signals names what fired per host.

tuning.reason: relay lookups alone are routine developer traffic
tuning.remove: delete the second `| EVAL signal = CASE(signal != ""` line

// Hunt: VS Code dev tunnel as remote access.
dataset = xdr_data
| filter (event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and (action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)code tunnel|vscode[.]dev/tunnel"
        or (action_process_image_name ~= "(?i)^code(-tunnel)?([.]exe)?$" and action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)tunnel")))
    or (event_type = ENUM.FILE and (action_file_name ~= "(?i)^code_tunnel[.]json$" and action_file_path ~= "(?i)[.]vscode-cli"
        or action_file_name ~= "(?i)^com[.]visualstudio[.]code[.]tunnel[.]plist$"))
    or (event_type = ENUM.NETWORK and dns_query_name ~= "(?i)(devtunnels[.]ms|rel[.]tunnels[.]api[.]visualstudio[.]com)$")
| alter signal = if(event_type = ENUM.PROCESS, "tunnel-command", if(event_type = ENUM.FILE, "tunnel-artifact-file", "relay-lookup"))
| comp values(signal) as signals, min(_time) as first_seen, max(_time) as last_seen by agent_hostname
| sort desc last_seen
queries.note: Finds tunnel commands, tunnel artifact files and relay lookups in xdr_data per host.

queries.query:
-- Hunt: VS Code dev tunnel as remote access; running tunnel processes and the artifacts a tunnel leaves (Windows and macOS).
SELECT 'tunnel-process' AS signal, name AS detail, cmdline AS evidence
FROM processes
WHERE (lower(name) IN ('code', 'code.exe', 'code-tunnel', 'code-tunnel.exe') AND cmdline LIKE '%tunnel%')
   OR cmdline LIKE '%code tunnel%' OR cmdline LIKE '%vscode.dev/tunnel%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'tunnel-artifact-file', filename, path
FROM file
WHERE path LIKE '/Users/%/.vscode-cli/code_tunnel.json'
   OR path LIKE 'C:\Users\%\.vscode-cli\code_tunnel.json'
   OR path = '/Library/LaunchAgents/com.visualstudio.code.tunnel.plist'
   OR path LIKE '/Users/%/Library/LaunchAgents/com.visualstudio.code.tunnel.plist'
queries.note: Local check for a running tunnel process and the code_tunnel.json or launch agent a tunnel leaves behind.

false_positive_notes: Dev tunnels are a supported Microsoft feature that developers use for cross-device debugging and remote containers, so a single invocation proves nothing. Abuse shows as persistence: a tunnel re-established daily or surviving reboots.

Correlate which account authorised the tunnel, often a personal GitHub identity rather than the corporate one, and whether inbound sessions arrive at times inconsistent with the employee's stated location.

title: Inbound RDP and VNC Listeners on an Employee Endpoint
summary: A laptop-farm machine has to accept inbound connections. This looks for an endpoint listening on, or accepting traffic on, remote-desktop and remote-access ports, adapting the port checks published by mattysplo.it.
description: Whatever the tooling, a laptop in a facilitator's rack must accept a connection from somewhere, and where it is not brokered by a cloud relay the machine has to be listening. The mattysplo.it write-up publishes narrow queries for inbound RDP on 3389 with private address space excluded, and broad ones for remote-access ports, processes, services and configuration files.

The port list is not only RDP: 3389 is RDP, 5900 to 5905 VNC, 5938 TeamViewer, 7070 AnyDesk and 8172 ScreenConnect, while 6568 appears in the source without a mapping. On macOS the equivalents are Screen Sharing and Remote Management on 5900 and Remote Login on 22.

This hunt keeps the port test, matched on the local side with private and loopback sources excluded, and leaves the process, service and configuration-file branches of the source to the remote-access sweep, where they share its false positives.
logic: Collect: network listen and accepted-connection events on Windows and macOS endpoints
Match: local port is 3389, 5900-5905, 5938, 7070, 8172 or 3283, with 22 and 6568 optional
Exclude: accepted connections whose remote address is private (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) or loopback
Report: hosts by local port and owning process, newest first
technique_scope: Remote Services (MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001 RDP, T1021.005 VNC) accepted inbound on an endpoint that should originate connections rather than receive them.

indicators.note: RDP, per the source's own protocol mapping.
VNC, per the source's own protocol mapping, which runs 5900 through 5905.
TeamViewer, per the source's own protocol mapping.
AnyDesk, per the source's own protocol mapping.
ScreenConnect, per the source's own protocol mapping.
Present in the source's port list but not assigned a protocol in its mapping. Commonly associated with AnyDesk elsewhere; this site does not assert that on the strength of a list membership.

queries.query:
// Hunt: inbound RDP, VNC and remote-access listeners on an employee endpoint (Windows and macOS).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted", "ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where LocalPort in (3389, 5900, 5901, 5902, 5903, 5904, 5905, 5938, 7070, 8172, 3283)
    // optional: Remote Login (22) is enabled deliberately by developers and IT teams
    or LocalPort == 22
    // optional: 6568 is in the source's port list without a protocol mapping
    or LocalPort == 6568
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
    or not(coalesce(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP), false) or RemoteIP startswith "127.")
| summarize Events = count(), RemoteAddresses = dcount(RemoteIP), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
        by DeviceName, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by LastSeen desc
queries.note: Listening and accepted-connection events per device, port and process; accepted connections from private or loopback addresses are excluded, listeners are kept.

tuning.reason: developers and IT teams enable SSH deliberately
tuning.remove: delete the // optional: Remote Login comment and the port 22 term next to it

tuning.reason: the source lists it without a protocol mapping
tuning.remove: delete the // optional: 6568 comment and the port 6568 term next to it

FROM logs-endpoint.events.network-*

// Hunt: inbound RDP, VNC and remote-access listeners. action_network_inbound is the field in the published mattysplo.it query; confirm it in your tenant.

queries.query:
-- Hunt: remote-desktop and remote-access listeners on this endpoint (Windows and macOS).
SELECT lp.port, lp.address, lp.protocol, p.name, p.path
FROM listening_ports lp
JOIN processes p USING (pid)
WHERE lp.port IN (3389, 5900, 5901, 5902, 5903, 5904, 5905, 5938, 7070, 8172, 3283)
   OR lp.port = 22  -- optional: Remote Login is enabled deliberately by developers and IT teams
   OR lp.port = 6568  -- optional: 6568 is in the source's port list without a protocol mapping
queries.note: Local listeners on the remote-access ports with the owning process, on Windows and macOS alike.

tuning.reason: SSH is enabled deliberately by developers, and 6568 has no protocol mapping in the source
tuning.remove: delete the two lines ending in -- optional

false_positive_notes: Where RDP to workstations is a supported help-desk path the narrow queries return that path; baseline and exclude legitimate jump hosts and support sources. The private-address exclusions do much of this work.
The process and file wildcards of the source, which match unrelated software, are left to the remote-access sweep and share its false positives.
On macOS, Screen Sharing and Remote Login are enabled deliberately by some users and IT teams, so compare against the management baseline.
Port 6568 appears in the source's list without a protocol mapping, and port 22 is enabled deliberately by many developers, so both are optional here.

title: Astrill VPN Egress on Corporate Authentication
summary: Astrill VPN is the anonymisation service most consistently associated with DPRK remote-worker fraud. This matches corporate sign-ins against its published exit addresses.
description: Astrill VPN appears in nearly every substantial report on this threat. Mandiant tags fourteen published addresses as Astrill exits, Unit 42 notes its popularity in China, and ReliaQuest observes that operators expose themselves when the tunnel drops, appearing one day through Astrill and the next on a Russian ISP. Spur has published a free list of roughly 2,400 addresses.

This is a commercial consumer VPN with an ordinary customer base, so an exit address is a reason to look, never a finding alone. Mandiant tags one Astrill address under Cogent (AS174), a transit network too broad to hunt on as an autonomous system; only the specific addresses apply.
logic: Collect: Entra ID and Okta sign-ins (interactive and non-interactive); optionally Windows and macOS process starts
Match: sign-in source address is one of the 14 Astrill exits Mandiant published, or is on the Spur Astrill list (watchlist or lookup)
Match: or (optional, weak) the Astrill client runs on an endpoint (astrill.exe, Astrill.app)
Report: users and source addresses with sign-in counts, newest first
technique_scope: Proxy/VPN egress obscuring the true origin of a session (MITRE ATT&CK T1090.003) in support of fraudulently obtained employment (T1078).

indicators.note: Tagged AstrillVPN in Mandiant's published indicator table (2024-09-23).

title: Egress from ISPs and Proxy Services Reported in DPRK Worker Cases
summary: The addresses operators appear on when the VPN is not in the way: Russian TTK ranges around Khabarovsk, China Unicom, and the commercial proxy and hosting services named in recent casework.
description: ReliaQuest's central observation is that operators slip: the same account authenticates through Astrill one day and from the Russian ISP TransTelekom the next. ReliaQuest publishes the TTK addresses seen in these campaigns, many in Khabarovsk, and China Unicom addresses found investigating North Korean incidents; Mandiant's table carries three of the same China Unicom addresses.

Huntress advises monitoring authentication through IPRoyal Proxy and infrastructure associated with WorkTitans B.V. in its 2026 casework. Where an employee's account has ever authenticated from any of these, that is a lead that does not depend on VPN attribution at all.

title: Unrelated Employees Authenticating from One Fixed-Line Address
summary: The signature of a laptop farm seen from the identity side: two or more employees who have nothing to do with each other, signing in from the same residential address.
description: ReliaQuest states the inference plainly: when two supposedly unrelated users in different environments connect from the exact same address, it strongly suggests a laptop farm. A facilitator racks employer-issued laptops in one residence and each egresses through its single connection; per the Department of Justice, Christina Chapman's operation ran more than ninety devices at one address.

Within a single employer the query is trivial, and its power grows when observations are shared between organisations, as across ReliaQuest's customers. ReliaQuest also notes that where one operator is uncovered several more are often present, up to ten inside one company within six months.
logic: Collect: successful Entra ID and Okta sign-ins with source address and user
Exclude: your own office and VPN egress ranges (replace the placeholder CIDR list)
Match: a source address used by 2 or more distinct users
Match: (optional) only accounts first seen in the last 120 days, which removes most household and shared-office noise
Report: addresses with their users, most users first
technique_scope: Valid-account misuse (MITRE ATT&CK T1078) surfaced by shared physical egress across accounts that should have no relationship.

queries.query:
// Hunt: unrelated employees signing in from one fixed-line address (a laptop-farm signature).
let CorporateEgress = dynamic([
    "198.51.100.0/24",   // replace with your own office and VPN egress ranges
    "203.0.113.0/24"
]);
// optional: restrict to accounts first seen in the last 120 days; the first sign-in is only a proxy for hire date and fails in a recently migrated tenant
let RecentHires = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(180d)
    | summarize FirstEverSignIn = min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName
    | where FirstEverSignIn > ago(120d)
    | project UserPrincipalName;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| where not(coalesce(ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, CorporateEgress), false))
// optional: recent hires only
| where UserPrincipalName in (RecentHires)
| summarize Users = dcount(UserPrincipalName), UserList = make_set(UserPrincipalName, 25),
            SignIns = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by IPAddress
| where Users >= 2
| sort by Users desc
queries.note: Addresses shared by two or more employees outside your own egress; fill the CorporateEgress ranges first or the output is meaningless.

tuning.reason: the first sign-in is only a proxy for hire date and fails in a recently migrated tenant
tuning.remove: delete the // optional: restrict line with the let RecentHires statement under it, and the // optional: recent hires only line with the where under it

queries.query:
// Hunt: unrelated employees signing in from one fixed-line address. Fields are read from the raw Entra ID or Okta JSON (ipAddress, userPrincipalName, alternateId), so no parser field name is assumed.
/"resultType"\s*:\s*"0"|"result"\s*:\s*"SUCCESS"/i
| regex("ipAddress[\" :]+(?<ip>[0-9a-fA-F:.]+)", strict=false)
| regex("(?:userPrincipalName|alternateId)[^a-zA-Z0-9_]+(?<user>[^\"]+)", strict=false)
| ip=* user=*
// replace the placeholder ranges with your own office and VPN egress ranges
| !cidr(ip, subnet=["198.51.100.0/24", "203.0.113.0/24"])
| groupBy([ip], function=[count(user, distinct=true, as=users), collect([user], limit=25), count(as=signIns), min(@timestamp, as=firstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=lastSeen)])
| users >= 2
| sort(users, order=desc)
queries.note: Same logic over ingested Entra ID or Okta events, reading the address and user from the raw JSON; the recent-hires restriction is not expressible without a first-seen lookup.

FROM logs-azure.signinlogs-*, logs-okta*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 90 days

| EVAL account = COALESCE(azure.signinlogs.properties.user_principal_name, user.name)
| STATS users = COUNT_DISTINCT(account), user_list = VALUES(account), sign_ins = COUNT(*), first_seen = MIN(@timestamp), last_seen = MAX(@timestamp) BY source.ip

false_positive_notes: Two employees at one address is usually a couple, a shared flat, a coworking space or a small satellite office. The corporate-egress exclusion has to be complete or the results are meaningless.

A genuine finding combines recent hire, unrelated accounts, a residential address and remote-access or KVM tooling. The recent-hire variant uses first sign-in as hire date, a proxy that fails in a recently migrated tenant.

title: Laptop Shipping Address and Sign-In Geography Against the Record
summary: Joins HR, asset-shipping and identity-provider data to find new hires whose laptop shipped away from their recorded address, or whose first month of sign-ins geolocates away from it, the control Mandiant and the FBI single out.
description: Every laptop-farm case begins with a shipment. The employer sends a device to the address the new hire gave, which in a DPRK operation belongs to a facilitator; the Department of Justice's June 2025 action describes facilitators hosting victim-company laptops at their residences and reaching them with KVM switches. The paper trail exists before the device boots.

State, Treasury and FBI guidance (2022) warns of developers who cannot receive items at the address on their identification; the FBI recommends signature-on-delivery (2023) and flags address or payment-platform changes during onboarding (2025). Mandiant's recommendation is implemented here: verify the laptop ships to, and geolocates at, the stated home.

Three joins do the work: the shipping address on the asset record against the HR home address; the state and country of the first thirty days of sign-ins against the record; and the location of the first MDM enrolment against the same. None needs endpoint telemetry, so it catches the hardware KVM case endpoint hunts cannot.
logic: Collect: Entra ID sign-ins (including Intune enrolment), the HR home address, and the asset shipping address
Exclude: your own office and VPN egress ranges (replace the placeholder CIDR list)
Match: no sign-in in the 30 days after start date comes from the home country, or none from the home state
Match: or an Intune enrolment sign-in in that window comes from outside the home state or country
Match: or the laptop's shipping postal code differs from the home postal code
Report: new hires with the countries, states and addresses seen, newest start date first
technique_scope: Valid-account misuse by a fraudulently hired employee (MITRE ATT&CK T1078) supported by hardware or software remote access from a location other than the one the identity claims (T1200, T1219); detection through provisioning and identity data rather than endpoint telemetry.

indicators.value: Laptop shipped to an address that is not the one on the employee's identification or HR record
indicators.note: State, Treasury and FBI guidance (2022) and FBI PSA231018 (2023).

indicators.value: First-month sign-ins geolocating to a different state or country from the address on file
indicators.note: Mandiant's recommendation to verify the laptop geolocates where the individual reports living (Google Cloud, 2024).

queries.query:
// Hunt: new hires whose first month of sign-ins, or first Intune enrolment, sits away from the home address on record.
// Needs a Sentinel watchlist NewHires from HR: HomeState as the region name, HomeCountry as the two-letter code the identity provider reports.
let CorporateEgress = dynamic([
    "198.51.100.0/24",   // replace with your own office and VPN egress ranges
    "203.0.113.0/24"
]);
let NewHires = _GetWatchlist('NewHires')
    | project UserPrincipalName = tostring(UserPrincipalName),
              HomeState = toupper(trim(@"\s+", tostring(HomeState))),
              HomeCountry = toupper(trim(@"\s+", tostring(HomeCountry))),
              StartDate = todatetime(StartDate);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(120d) and ResultType == "0"
| where not(coalesce(ipv4_is_in_any_range(IPAddress, CorporateEgress), false))
| join kind=inner NewHires on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated between (StartDate .. (StartDate + 30d))
| extend SignInState = toupper(trim(@"\s+", tostring(LocationDetails.state))),
         SignInCountry = toupper(trim(@"\s+", tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)))
| where isnotempty(SignInCountry)
| summarize SignIns = count(), States = make_set(SignInState), Countries = make_set(SignInCountry),
            EnrolmentAwayFromHome = countif(AppDisplayName =~ "Microsoft Intune Enrollment" and (SignInCountry != HomeCountry or SignInState != HomeState)),
            Addresses = make_set(IPAddress, 20)
        by UserPrincipalName, HomeState, HomeCountry, StartDate
| where set_has_element(Countries, HomeCountry) == false or set_has_element(States, HomeState) == false or EnrolmentAwayFromHome > 0
| project UserPrincipalName, StartDate, HomeCountry, HomeState, Countries, States, EnrolmentAwayFromHome, SignIns, Addresses
| sort by StartDate desc
queries.note: Rows are new hires whose first-month sign-ins or Intune enrolment sit away from the recorded home; a mismatch is a question for the hiring manager, not an alert.

queries.query:
```Placeholders: index=identity holds Okta, Entra ID or ms:aad:signin events with action, src_ip, user and app extracted; new_hires.csv carries user, start_time (epoch), home_state and home_country in the full-name form iplocation returns; asset_shipments.csv and employee_directory.csv come from the asset system and HR.```
| inputlookup asset_shipments.csv
| lookup employee_directory.csv employee_id OUTPUT home_postal_code
| eval ship_postal_code=upper(trim(ship_postal_code)), home_postal_code=upper(trim(home_postal_code))
| where isnotnull(home_postal_code) AND ship_postal_code!=home_postal_code
| eval signal="shipping-address-mismatch", subject=employee_id, detail=ship_postal_code." shipped, ".home_postal_code." on record", when=ship_date
| append
    [ search index=identity (sourcetype=okta OR sourcetype=azuread OR sourcetype="ms:aad:signin") action=success earliest=-120d
      | where NOT (cidrmatch("198.51.100.0/24", src_ip) OR cidrmatch("203.0.113.0/24", src_ip))
      | lookup new_hires.csv user OUTPUT start_time home_state home_country
      | eval home_state=trim(home_state), home_country=trim(home_country)
      | where isnotnull(start_time) AND _time>=start_time AND _time<=(start_time+2592000)
      | iplocation src_ip
      | eval enrol_away=if(app="Microsoft Intune Enrollment" AND (lower(Country)!=lower(home_country) OR lower(Region)!=lower(home_state)), 1, 0)
      | stats count AS sign_ins values(Region) AS regions values(Country) AS countries values(src_ip) AS addresses max(enrol_away) AS enrol_away BY user, home_state, home_country, start_time
      | where isnull(mvfind(countries, "(?i)^".home_country."$")) OR isnull(mvfind(regions, "(?i)^".home_state."$")) OR enrol_away=1
      | eval signal="signin-away-from-home", subject=user, detail=mvjoin(countries, "/")." vs ".home_country, when=start_time ]
| table subject, signal, detail, when
| sort - when
queries.note: Combines the shipping-address mismatch and the sign-in mismatch in one result keyed by employee; replace the placeholder egress ranges and lookups first.

false_positive_notes: People move, ship to a workplace or a relative, and travel in their first month, so a mismatch is a question for the hiring manager rather than an alert.
Corporate VPN egress geolocates every sign-in to the concentrator and must be excluded, or the join run against the pre-VPN device address the identity provider records.
Geolocation of consumer addresses is accurate to the state more often than the city, hence the state and country comparison. The hunt is only as good as the HR export.
If the address on file was never verified against an identity document, comparing against it proves little; run the shipping check against the document address.

title: Concurrent Multi-Geography Sessions on One Identity
summary: Impossible-travel and overlapping-session logic aimed at the specific case where a laptop physically sits in one country while the person operating it is in another.
description: DPRK IT-worker fraud relies on facilitators hosting laptop farms, residences or offices racked with employer-issued laptops, remotely controlled from overseas through commercial remote-access tools or hardware KVMs and frequently egressing through Astrill VPN. Christina Chapman's 2025 sentencing, over a farm of more than ninety devices used to defraud 309 companies, is the documented example.

Whatever the transport, the geography does not reconcile: the facilitator's side checks in from where the farm is while the operator signs in from where they are, so one account appears in two countries at once. This hunt groups successful sign-ins by account and hour and reports any account seen in two or more countries.
logic: Collect: successful interactive sign-ins from Entra ID (SigninLogs) or Okta, last 30 days
Match: the same account succeeds from two or more countries inside one hour (country taken from the source IP)
Exclude: corporate egress and sanctioned VPN addresses
Report: account, hour, countries, addresses and sign-in count, newest first
technique_scope: Remote Access Tools abuse (MITRE ATT&CK T1219, T1219.002) combined with impossible-travel and valid-account misuse (T1078) consistent with laptop-farm operations.

queries.query:
// Replace the placeholder addresses with the organisation's corporate egress and sanctioned VPN ranges.
let CorporateEgress = dynamic(["203.0.113.10", "203.0.113.11"]);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| where IPAddress !in (CorporateEgress)
| extend Country = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| where isnotempty(Country)
| summarize Countries = make_set(Country), Addresses = make_set(IPAddress, 10), SignIns = count()
    by UserPrincipalName, Hour = bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where array_length(Countries) >= 2
| sort by Hour desc
queries.note: Each row is one account that succeeded from two or more countries inside one fixed hour; replace the placeholder egress addresses before running it.

queries.query:
```sourcetype placeholders: ms:aad:signin (Entra ID, interactive) and okta; user, src_ip and action follow the CIM Authentication model```
```replace the placeholder addresses with the organisation's corporate egress and sanctioned VPN ranges```
index=identity (sourcetype="ms:aad:signin" OR sourcetype=okta) action=success earliest=-30d
| search NOT src_ip IN ("203.0.113.10", "203.0.113.11")
| iplocation src_ip
| where isnotnull(Country) AND Country!=""
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(Country) AS country_count values(Country) AS countries values(src_ip) AS addresses count AS sign_ins BY user _time
| where country_count>=2
| sort 0 - _time
| convert ctime(_time)
queries.note: Each row is one account seen in two or more countries inside one fixed hour, from Entra ID or Okta sign-ins.

queries.query:
FROM logs-azure.signinlogs-*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 30 days AND event.outcome == "success" AND source.geo.country_iso_code IS NOT NULL
| WHERE NOT CIDR_MATCH(source.ip, "203.0.113.0/24")
| EVAL hour = DATE_TRUNC(1 hour, @timestamp)
| STATS countries = COUNT_DISTINCT(source.geo.country_iso_code), country_list = VALUES(source.geo.country_iso_code), addresses = VALUES(source.ip), sign_ins = COUNT(*) BY azure.signinlogs.properties.user_principal_name, hour
| WHERE countries >= 2
| SORT hour DESC
| LIMIT 200
queries.note: Each row is one Entra ID account seen in two or more countries inside one fixed hour; replace the placeholder 203.0.113.0/24 with the corporate egress ranges.

queries.query:
// Entra ID sign-ins parsed into ECS-style fields (user.name, source.ip, event.outcome); replace the placeholder egress range.
event.outcome=success
| !cidr(source.ip, subnet="203.0.113.0/24")
| ipLocation(field=source.ip)
| source.ip.country=*
| bucket(span=1h, field=user.name, function=[count(as=sign_ins), count(source.ip.country, distinct=true, as=countries), collect([source.ip.country, source.ip])])
| countries >= 2
| sort(_bucket, order=desc)

false_positive_notes: Legitimate travel, corporate VPN egress and sanctioned remote-support sessions all trigger this, and most identity platforms already ship an impossible-travel detection tuned into silence long ago; where the tenant has Microsoft Entra ID Protection's atypical-travel alerts, read those alongside this result.
Hardware KVM usage never appears in endpoint process telemetry, so pair this hunt with the hardware hunts and with physical-asset and shipping-address review, not EDR alone.
Mandiant recommends verifying that a corporate laptop geolocates where the employee says they live, a control rather than a query that is worth implementing alongside this.

Fixed hourly bins miss a pair of sign-ins that straddles an hour boundary, and mobile carriers and consumer VPNs geolocate to the wrong country often enough that every hit needs a human look at the two addresses.

title: VDO.Ninja (OBS.Ninja) Screen Relay and Interview-Support Web Services
summary: Browser artifacts of the screen-relay and audio/video test services Huntress recovered from a suspected DPRK worker's laptop, including the vdo.ninja push URL used to stream the host's screen out.
description: VDO.Ninja is a legitimate browser tool that carries a webcam, microphone or screen share over WebRTC into OBS or another production application. On the laptop Huntress examined it was doing something else: a push URL with the screenshare parameter set, recovered from the Chrome cache, streaming the host's own screen out to whoever held the matching view link.

Around it sat services that make sense only for someone rehearsing a call they will not attend: microphone and webcam test sites, an address checker consulted minutes before a Zoom meeting, peer-to-peer file transfer, and a public code-sharing site holding recurring Zoom invitations with embedded passwords. Huntress recommends hunting the whole cluster rather than any single service.
The service was called OBS.Ninja until a 2022 rebrand and that name still circulates in setup guides and bookmarks, so the queries below match obs.ninja alongside the current domain.
logic: Collect: DNS lookups and network connections on Windows and macOS endpoints, plus proxy URLs where they are ingested
Match: destination host is VDO.Ninja or OBS.Ninja, a mic or webcam test site, ip.me, Toffeeshare, SendGB or Codeshare
Report: devices reaching 2 or more distinct services in 90 days, or one VDO.Ninja URL with push= and screenshare
technique_scope: Screen capture and exfiltration over a legitimate web service (MITRE ATT&CK T1113, T1567), supporting impersonation during video interviews and meetings.

indicators.note: Browser-based WebRTC relay; Huntress assessed its use here as screen capture of the host.

Former domain of the same service, which rebranded from OBS.Ninja to VDO.Ninja in 2022 as the project's own repository records. Huntress reports vdo.ninja; obs.ninja is carried here because a proxy or EDR rule written against one name does not match the other.
Microphone test site accessed minutes after the IP-KVM audio interface registered (Huntress).
Webcam and microphone test site (Huntress).
Microphone test site (Huntress).
Address-checking service accessed minutes before joining a Zoom meeting (Huntress).
Peer-to-peer file transfer, used with a Chrome extension that records browser tab video and audio (Huntress). The domain is the service's own; Huntress names the service rather than a URL.
File-transfer service; a third party uploaded a file that the user then downloaded to C:\asset (Huntress).
Public code-sharing site used to publish recurring Zoom meetings with embedded passwords (Huntress).

title: Virtual Cameras and Video-Call Obfuscation Tooling
summary: Software and hardware that lets an arbitrary video feed be presented to Zoom or Teams as a webcam, including real-time face-swap tooling, which is how an operator attends a call as somebody else.
description: Operators avoid cameras where they can and substitute for them where they cannot. Mandiant records reluctance to turn cameras on; ReliaQuest describes deepfakes when live interaction is unavoidable; DTEX names OBS and ManyCam; Microsoft names face-swap and voice-changing software. Huntress found the hardware version, a Guermok USB capture card registered as a webcam.

The software half of this now has an open-source form that costs nothing and leaves traces of its own: Deep-Live-Cam swaps a face into a live video feed from a single still image, is fed to a conferencing client through a capture or virtual-camera tool, and pulls two named ONNX models before it can run at all.

This hunt looks for all of it on Windows and macOS: virtual-camera and face-swap software, the face-swap model files, and capture hardware in device telemetry, best correlated against the times the employee was on a call.
logic: Collect: process starts, file writes and USB enrolments on Windows and macOS, where the product records them
Match: process is OBS, ManyCam or XSplit, or its command line names Deep-Live-Cam
Match: or a file named inswapper_128* or gfpgan-1024* (.onnx) is written
Match: or a USB device is the Guermok capture card (VID_345F PID_2130, or its UltraSemi and MacroSilicon names)
Exclude: devices of media-production and training staff
Report: devices with the signals seen, newest first; the models and the card are strong, a tool alone is weak
technique_scope: Impersonation during live video interaction through video-input manipulation, supporting fraudulently obtained employment (MITRE ATT&CK T1078) and identity masquerading (T1036).

indicators.note: Named by DTEX in the DPRK IT-worker context; its virtual camera presents any composited scene as a webcam.
Virtual camera and video-switching software named by DTEX.

Guermok USB3 Video capture card (VID_345F, PID_2130) that registered as a webcam, letting any video streamed through it be sent as camera input to Zoom (Huntress). The card also enumerates under its chipset vendors' names, UltraSemi and MacroSilicon, on some hosts; the query matches both (this site's observation, 18 September 2026).

Open-source application that swaps a face into a live video feed from a single still image, paired with a screen-capture or virtual-camera tool to reach a conferencing client. Microsoft names face-swap software categorically in its Jasper Sleet reporting and Unit 42 demonstrated that a working real-time deepfake takes about an hour to assemble from tooling of this kind; neither report names this project, which is listed as one of the widely available implementations of the technique rather than as an indicator recovered from a case.
Source repository for Deep-Live-Cam, which runs as python run.py from a working copy rather than under an executable name worth listing.
Face-swap model Deep-Live-Cam requires in its models folder; roughly 300 MB of model data is fetched on first run (project documentation).
Face-enhancement model Deep-Live-Cam requires alongside the swap model (project documentation).

queries.query:
// Replace the placeholder with the devices of media-production and training staff.
let MediaDevices = dynamic(["media-workstation-01"]);
let VirtualCameraImages = dynamic(["obs64.exe", "obs32.exe", "manycam.exe", "xsplit.core.exe"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where ProcessCommandLine contains "Deep-Live-Cam"
        // optional: OBS, ManyCam and XSplit are ordinary software, the weakest part of this hunt
        or FileName in~ (VirtualCameraImages)
        or FolderPath contains "/OBS.app/" or FolderPath contains "/ManyCam.app/"
   | extend Signal = iff(ProcessCommandLine contains "Deep-Live-Cam", "deep-live-cam", "virtual-camera-tool"), Detail = FileName
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal, Detail),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
   | where FileName startswith "inswapper_128" or FileName startswith "gfpgan-1024"
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "deep-live-cam-model", Detail = FileName),
  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where ActionType == "PnpDeviceConnected"
   | extend Fields = parse_json(AdditionalFields)
   | extend Description = tostring(Fields.DeviceDescription), UsbId = tostring(Fields.DeviceId)
   | where Description has "Guermok" or UsbId contains "VID_345F&PID_2130"
        // optional: chipset names shared by many generic capture cards
        or Description has_any ("UltraSemi", "MacroSilicon", "USB3 Video")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "capture-card", Detail = Description)
| where DeviceName !in~ (MediaDevices)
| summarize Signals = make_set(Signal), Details = make_set(Detail, 10), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| sort by LastSeen desc
queries.note: Devices showing any virtual-camera, face-swap or capture-card signal, with the signals listed so the strong ones can be read first.

This is a lead generator whose value comes from correlation with reluctance to appear on camera, an IP-KVM on the same host, or mismatched identity documents. Alone it will return your marketing department.

The face-swap half is the exception: a real-time face-replacement application on a corporate endpoint has few business uses that survive being asked about, and its model files are not downloaded by accident.
