title: NetKey and OConnect: DPRK Internal-Network Clients on an Endpoint
summary: Process names, install paths and vendor directories for NetKey and OConnect, which Flare assesses are used to authenticate to North Korean internal networks, with the internal URL paths that accompany them.
description: Flare's infiltrator research records two applications, NetKey and OConnect, on machines it assesses belong to North Korean IT workers, and says both are highly likely used to authenticate operators to North Korean internal networks. Neither appears to be sold commercially. They are Windows products, so this hunt covers Windows endpoints only.

The strongest artefact is the install directory: Flare records vendor folders STN Corp and rb corp in Program Files (x86). Flare also documents two internal web applications whose URL paths, such as machine_info_new or a netkey_id parameter, can be searched; their private addresses are deliberately not listed. IP Messenger is weaker, supporting evidence only.

Chollima Group's October 2024 analysis of infostealer logs from five DPRK IT worker sets found NetKey on every one, v4.0 and v4.1 on four Khabarovsk hosts and v5.0 on a Hong Kong host, and assesses it as the utility that authenticates access to Kwangmyong, North Korea's intranet. It does not mention OConnect, STN Corp or rb corp.
logic: Collect: process starts on Windows endpoints, installed programs through osquery, and proxy requests
Match: a process runs from an STN Corp or rb corp folder, or is named NetKey.exe or OConnect.exe (the bare names are weaker)
Match: or an installed product, vendor or publisher is NetKey, OConnect, STN Corp or rb corp (software inventory)
Match: or a request URL holds an internal application path (/machine_info, /network_reports, /blocked_urls, netkey_id=, /register-port)
Report: devices with the signals seen, first and last time, newest first
technique_scope: Valid-account misuse through fraudulent employment (MITRE ATT&CK T1078), with operator-side tooling for authenticating to attacker-controlled infrastructure (T1133) and reconnaissance of that infrastructure over internal web applications (T1083).
data_sources: Installed-software inventory and registry Uninstall keys

indicators.note: Recorded by Flare on a machine it assesses belongs to a North Korean IT worker. The vendor directory is what makes this high-fidelity, so match on the path rather than on the executable name alone.
As above, for the 6.0.0 install.
The NetKey binary installed under a second vendor directory, rb corp, in a folder named for OConnect. Flare records the two products shipping alongside one another.
The two Program Files (x86) vendor folders Flare observed. A directory named for either is the anchor for this hunt: neither corresponds to software a corporate estate would normally hold.
Observed running on machines Flare assesses belong to North Korean IT workers. Weaker on its own than the full path, and worth corroborating against the install location.
As above. OConnect is a generic enough name that a bare process match needs the vendor directory to confirm it.

Flare records 4.1, 5.0 and 5.1 as installed on operator machines. Chollima Group independently records 4.0 and 4.1 on four hosts and 5.0 on a fifth, from infostealer logs captured in 2020 and 2021, which is where 4.0 comes from. Useful against software-inventory data where process telemetry has not been retained.
The OConnect versions Flare records as installed.

Paths on the internal application Flare calls the RB Site, whose page is titled Add Machine Info. The private address that served them is not listed; generic paths Flare also records, such as login, user and payment, are omitted because they match most web applications.

Paths on the NetkeyRegister application, which Flare observed on port 8000. The netkey_id parameter ties it to the NetKey client; generic paths such as register, change-password and upload are omitted.
Open-source, serverless local-network messaging application Flare records as a communication tool among these operators. Legitimate software with ordinary uses, so supporting evidence only.

queries.query:
// NetKey and OConnect: process, software inventory and proxy signals, reported per device
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where FolderPath contains @"\STN Corp\"
        or FolderPath contains @"\rb corp\"
        // optional: other vendors also use the names NetKey and OConnect
        or FileName in~ ("NetKey.exe", "OConnect.exe")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "process", Detail = FolderPath),
  (DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
   | where SoftwareName has_any ("NetKey", "OConnect") or SoftwareVendor has_any ("STN Corp", "rb corp")
        // optional: IP Messenger is legitimate open-source software, supporting evidence only
        or SoftwareName has_any ("IP Messenger", "IPMsg")
   | project Timestamp = now(), DeviceName, Signal = "inventory", Detail = strcat(SoftwareVendor, " ", SoftwareName, " ", SoftwareVersion)),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where RequestURL contains "/machine_info"
        or RequestURL contains "/network_reports"
        or RequestURL contains "/blocked_urls"
        or RequestURL contains "netkey_id="
        or RequestURL contains "/register-port"
        or RequestURL contains "/register-service"
   | project Timestamp = TimeGenerated, DeviceName = SourceIP, Signal = "url", Detail = RequestURL)
| summarize Signals = make_set(Signal), Events = count(), Examples = make_set(Detail, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| sort by LastSeen desc
queries.note: One row per device across process, software-inventory and proxy records, where a process from a vendor directory is the strongest hit and the inventory rows carry no time.

tuning.part: the bare process names NetKey.exe and OConnect.exe
tuning.reason: other vendors also use these names, so the vendor directory is the real anchor
tuning.remove: delete the `// optional: other vendors` line and the `or FileName in~ ("NetKey.exe", "OConnect.exe")` line below it.

tuning.reason: IP Messenger is legitimate open-source software and counts only as supporting evidence
tuning.remove: delete the `// optional: IP Messenger` line and the `or SoftwareName has_any ("IP Messenger", "IPMsg")` line below it.

queries.query:
```index=endpoint holds Windows process events (Security 4688 or Sysmon 1) with the Endpoint fields, index=proxy holds proxy events; the vendor directory is read from the command line because no image-path field is assumed```
(index=endpoint OR index=proxy) earliest=-90d
| eval cmd=replace(lower(process), "\\\\", "/"), proc=lower(process_name), web=lower(url)
| eval signal=case(
    match(cmd, "/stn corp/|/rb corp/"), "process",
    ```optional: other vendors also use the names NetKey and OConnect```
    in(proc, "netkey.exe", "oconnect.exe"), "process",
    match(web, "/machine_info|/network_reports|/blocked_urls|netkey_id=|/register-port|/register-service"), "url",

title: logs-bin and logs-dump: Republished Keylogger Packages on npm
summary: Two npm packages published by one maintainer that republish the node-global-key-listener library under new names, one of them carrying a Windows binary thirty-two times the size of the legitimate one it replaces.
description: A May 2026 researcher post named logs-dump and logs-bin as a live DPRK keylogger on npm. The registry confirms one maintainer, topnotcher847, publishing both on the same day in June 2025 under bland descriptions. Both republish the node-global-key-listener library, its build output and its three key-server binaries, under their own names rather than depending on it.

The packages are not equally interesting. Every binary in logs-dump, and the Linux binary in logs-bin, is byte-identical to upstream. Only logs-bin replaces the Windows binary, at 75 MB against upstream's 2.3 MB, thirty-two times the size, which a rebuild of the same source does not produce. That file is the one indicator worth alerting on.

The obvious mistake is hashing both packages' binaries. The researcher cites an antivirus detection on WinKeyServer.exe without saying which copy was scanned, and logs-dump's copy is the upstream artefact every legitimate consumer installs. A keylistening binary trips antivirus honestly, so the score says nothing about DPRK involvement.
logic: Collect: file and process events on Windows, macOS and Linux; proxy requests; packages, hashes and lockfiles via osquery and YARA
Match: the SHA-256 8587edcb... of the replaced WinKeyServer.exe from logs-bin@3.11.14 is written, run or found on disk (alert on this alone)
Match: or a file lands under node_modules/logs-bin or node_modules/logs-dump, or either package is installed (exposure only)
Match: or a proxy request fetches either package from registry.npmjs.org, or a lockfile or manifest names either package (exposure only)
Report: devices with the signal kinds seen, first and last time, newest first
technique_scope: Supply-chain compromise through a public package registry (MITRE ATT&CK T1195.002), delivering an input-capture capability (T1056.001) to a developer workstation.
data_sources: Software composition analysis and SBOM inventory

indicators.note: Published 2025-06-04 by topnotcher847. Two versions, latest 1.7.5. Republishes node-global-key-listener in full; its binaries are byte-identical to the legitimate upstream release, so the package name is the indicator and its file hashes are not.
Published 2025-06-04 by the same maintainer. Eight versions, latest 3.11.14. This is the package carrying a replaced Windows binary.
The registry account behind both packages. Any further package published by it is worth treating the same way.
The maintainer address the npm registry publishes for that account. It is registry metadata rather than a value recovered from the payload.

bin/WinKeyServer.exe from logs-bin@3.11.14, 75,105,792 bytes. This is the only binary in either package that differs from the legitimate upstream release, and it is thirty-two times its size. Alert on this one.
Where the binary lands after an install. The same file names appear under node-global-key-listener for legitimate consumers of that library, so the parent directory is what separates them.

queries.query:
// logs-bin and logs-dump: the replaced binary by hash, optionally the package paths and registry downloads
union
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA256 == "8587edcb8c9e384a7c3b4726a23e93d0bd2fdd2267984a7982484ee327983902"
        // optional: logs-dump's binaries equal upstream, so a path hit shows exposure only
        or FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)[/\\]node_modules[/\\]logs-(bin|dump)[/\\]"
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "file", Detail = FolderPath),
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA256 == "8587edcb8c9e384a7c3b4726a23e93d0bd2fdd2267984a7982484ee327983902"
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal = "process", Detail = FolderPath)
  // optional: a registry download shows exposure only
  , (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where RequestURL contains "registry.npmjs.org/logs-bin" or RequestURL contains "registry.npmjs.org/logs-dump"
   | project Timestamp = TimeGenerated, DeviceName = SourceIP, Signal = "registry", Detail = RequestURL)
| summarize Signals = make_set(Signal), Events = count(), Examples = make_set(Detail, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| sort by LastSeen desc
queries.note: Alert on the SHA-256 hit alone, and read a path or registry row as historical exposure to investigate.

title: OtterCookie C2 by Its Three-Port Fingerprint
summary: The current OtterCookie variant splits its traffic across three ports on one host, 8085, 8086 and 8087, behind an Express server, which makes its command-and-control servers findable in internet scan data before any sample points at them.
description: @unpacker on X observed that the OtterCookie variant used in Contagious Interview gives each job its own port: 8086 for primary file exfiltration, 8085 for secondary exfiltration, and 8087 for the Socket.IO command channel, clipboard capture and log upload. A server answering on all three with Express is an unusual shape, and the published examples cluster on one hosting provider.

The Censys query finds hosts presenting all three ports with Express. Compare the results with egress, proxy and EDR network logs: a developer workstation talking to one of them on any of the three ports is the lead. The indicator list carries the hosts the researcher's query returned and those a second researcher added from telemetry.
logic: Collect: network connections from endpoints, firewalls and flow logs on Windows, macOS and Linux; Censys scan data for the fingerprint
Match: one source reaches 2 or more of the ports 8085, 8086 and 8087 on a single public address
Match: or a connection to one of the eleven listed fingerprint hosts on one of those ports (matches, not confirmed infections)
Match: or, in Censys, a host runs Express on all of 8085, 8086 and 8087, which lists new candidates before any traffic
Report: sources with the address, ports reached, first and last time, newest first
technique_scope: Command and control over an application-layer protocol (MITRE ATT&CK T1071.001) and exfiltration over the C2 channel (T1041) by the OtterCookie malware in Contagious Interview intrusions.

host.services: (port = 8085 and (software.vendor = "express" or software.product = "express"))

queries.note: Ports are integers, the Express clause is bound to each port within one service, both vendor and product fields are accepted because Censys may record Express under either, and the post's RouterHosting LLC pin is left out to catch the same build elsewhere.

false_positive_notes: Express on high ports is common in development and staging, and three adjacent ports open together will occasionally be a legitimate multi-service deployment.
A match is a host worth checking against your own logs, not a finding on its own.
The indicator list is a set of fingerprint matches rather than servers seen in a confirmed infection.
